This month, two concerts will showcase the results of a bold country-wide effort led by music teachers who believe every student—no matter how old or how advanced—can make classical music their own. Over the past year, thousands of youngsters have picked apart ten iconic works, everything from a Beethoven symphony to a Chopin nocturne, and now they’re ready to share what the music says to them.

The chosen pieces, whittled down by top conductors and classroom veterans, trace four centuries of style, giving players a crash course in musical history while leaving room for personal flair. Some will step onstage alone with a violin or electric guitar; others will arrive in drumming circles and string quartets. Each act is a new coat of paint on an old masterpiece.

James Morris, one of the teachers steering the project, puts it simply: “We want kids to treat these scores like playground equipment—climb on, swing around, and see what tricks they can invent.” The goal isn’t perfect imitation; it’s discovery.

The Royal Albert Hall, long a champion of young musicians, has thrown open its doors for the occasion. Its famous dome has heard everything from Mahler to the Beatles, but these nights belong to the next generation. Cameras and radio mics will capture the energy so anyone tuning in from home can hear fresh takes on timeless tunes.

Organisers trust the ripple effect will reach far beyond the performers, tempting even the “I don’t do classical” crowd to lean in and listen. After all, when teenagers reimagine Tchaikovsky, the music feels less like a museum piece and more like a living conversation—one the whole country is invited to join.

Walsh insists that protecting the lifeline services the city depends on will demand bold, even unprecedented steps. He spoke out after Westminster slashed the budget again, cuts he warns will bite deep into everyday life.

“We’re in uncharted water, so the old rulebook won’t keep us afloat,” he told last week’s emergency council session. “I respect the law, but when the cupboards are bare you look everywhere for food, even places you’re told you can’t go. If that means drafting a budget that technically breaks the rules, so be it.”

He was quick to add that an “illegal budget” isn’t a licence to splash cash. Instead, the council could deliberately breach statutory spending caps, absorb the fines or court dates, and still keep libraries, meals-on-wheels and youth centres alive.

The remark split the chamber—and the city. Some councillors and residents cheered, saying services are already threadbare. Others fear another leap into legal and financial quicksand.

“I know the risks,” Walsh replied. “But they’re smaller than the human cost of closing another children’s centre or letting pensioners sit in the cold.”

He finished with a challenge: “We were elected to look after Liverpool. If we won’t stand up when the axe falls, who will? We may have to defy the government’s austerity playbook to save the communities it’s dismantling.”

The council now faces weeks of bitter debate, and local pundits say the issue could decide May’s elections. Every move Liverpool makes will be watched—by residents, national media and ministers waiting to pounce.

Your story feels like a quiet room where the walls are listening. On the face of it, people are only passing the salt or closing the curtains, but every syllable creaks with something they daren’t say aloud. The pauses yawn wider than the speeches, and the real conversation is happening in the tight smiles and unfinished sentences. Somewhere off-stage, an answer is missing, and that absence keeps the air humming.

Just like Pinter, you let the ordinary tilt into the unsettling: the armchair that suddenly looks like a trap, the old friend whose joke lands like a threat. A child’s toy left on the table glows with meaning no one wants to name. You don’t explain; you let the silence do the talking, and it speaks in goose-bumps. We leave the page carrying the same unease we bring back from half-remembered dreams about people we thought we knew.

Stay with that tone. Keep the kettle boiling while the danger stays just out of sight; let small talk feel like walking barefoot on glass. Keep asking why we sit opposite the people we love and still can’t find the right word. Keep us leaning forward, hunting for clues in every hush, until the final full stop closes the door—quietly, maddeningly—before we’re ready to leave the room.

1. Conductor, Philharmonics: “This hall sounds like you’re sitting inside a cello—every note just blooms around you.”

2. Margo Davis, Soprano: “Walk through the doors and the place practically whispers every legend that’s sung here before you—goosebumps every time.”

3. Ethan O’Brien, Cello: “You’re close enough to catch someone holding their breath on the big screen; that closeness is pure magic.”

4. Alexander Boone, Violinist: “Sharing the boards with my heroes? Pinch-me stuff—childhood daydream turned real.”

5. Fiona Greenspan, Flute: “The air itself seems to hum back at you; it’s like the Hall joins the tune.”

6. Matthew Hill, Trombone: “These listeners don’t just hear—they lean in, live every phrase. You feel them riding the wave with you.”

7. Julia Orff, Percussion: “Backstage buzz feels like the building’s heartbeat—centuries of greats queued up right where you’re standing.”

8. Isla Redmond, Clarinet: “It’s more than bricks and velvet; it’s Britain’s musical crown in stone form.”

9. Graham Simmons, Bass: “Under that vast dome you shrink and swell at once—tiny cog, huge story.”

10. Amelia Turner, Piano: “The minutes before the lights rise taste like electricity—equal parts terror and thrill.”

11. Benjamin Daniels, Conductor: “The downstroke lands, the chord rings, and you remember why we do this: to add one more brushstroke to forever.”

Gunmen thought to be Taliban slipped into a police station late at night, trading fire with officers for hours before Afghan troops finally retook the building at dawn.

Officials say the breach was made possible by an insider: a man who had served on the force long enough to know the building’s layout and alarm codes. Wearing a police uniform, he disabled the security system, opened the gate, and joined the assault. The shoot-out left several officers dead and others wounded; the exact toll is still unclear amid the confusion.

Since U.S. and NATO troops pulled out, the Taliban have pushed to recapture ground across Afghanistan, and Lashkar Gah—the capital of Helmand—sits high on their list because of its roads and tax revenue. Provincial police chief Haji Mirwais Noorzai admitted the attacker “had been one of us,” giving him access to sensitive details.

An investigation is now under way, he said, and recruitment vetting will be tightened. “We owe it to the families of the fallen,” Noorzai added. “This pain reminds us our checkpoints are only as strong as the trust inside them.”

Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid claimed the raid on social media, praising the “successful martyrdom operation.”

The UN mission in Afghanistan denounced the incident as “a serious violation of the laws of war,” while diplomats warn that without swift reforms the country’s fragile security gains could unravel even further.

Workers are walking out over a government plan to raise the retirement age, hike pension contributions, and shrink future payouts for everyone in the public service—from border guards to clerks. Airports, seaports, and border crossings are bracing for long lines and missed connections.

Union bosses call the package “pension robbery” and swear to fight it. Their bottom line: people who keep the country running shouldn’t be asked to pay more, work longer, and retire on less.

Ministers counter that longer lives and stretched budgets leave no choice. They insist the reformed schemes will still look generous beside most private-sector plans.

Travellers should pack patience: passport control could take twice as long, visa counters may close, and luggage might crawl through customs.

Talks so far have gone nowhere, and union ballots for more stoppages are already circulating. If Westminster refuses to budge, sporadic strikes could stretch into summer.

The dispute is the sharpest flashpoint yet in the wider clash over austerity. With ageing populations everywhere, the fight over who shoulders the cost is only getting started.

Critics say the government is picking on modest-paid nurses, cleaners, and guards instead of chasing tax loopholes. For many, the extra contributions will feel like a second pay cut.

On the picket lines the message is simple: come back to the table with a deal that safeguards dignity in retirement without stripping services bare. As the clock ticks down, no one can say which side will blink first.

Arctic Terns—listed as “least concern” by the IUCN—still make the planet’s longest commute, flying from pole to pole every year. So when the environment department issued a stark warning this week, it was a reminder that even common birds can slide toward trouble fast.

While not officially endangered, the terns’ numbers have quietly dropped. Plastic in the ocean, warming seas, vanishing nesting beaches and, sometimes, people who shoot or harass them all add up.

New rules are now on the table. Under existing wildlife laws, anyone who deliberately hurts a tern risks heavy fines or even jail time, depending on the offense. Officers say they’ll enforce the statutes, not just park them on paper.

Beyond penalties, officials want a culture shift. They’re asking neighbors to call in anything suspicious—off-leash dogs on nesting islands, fireworks near colonies, or drones buzzing overhead. “Think of it as neighborhood watch, just with feathers,” one biologist said.

Groups like Audubon Alaska already run with that idea: each summer volunteers camp near tern colonies, counting chicks and shooing away careless beachgoers. The state hopes to copy and expand those grassroots efforts.

The department closed its briefing with a simple plea: every creature, from the showy tern to the humble clam, holds a thread in the web we all depend on. Cut enough threads and the whole thing frays. So tread lightly, speak up, and leave the birds room to wing their wild, endless loop around the globe.

Even though their gathering has stirred up strong feelings, the organisers say they’re not out to attack anyone. They insist the point isn’t to swipe at LGBTQ+ people or roll back their rights, only to speak up for the traditional picture of family and marriage they were raised with.

“These ideas are part of the glue that’s held our communities together,” said John Smith, who’s speaking for the group. “We’re not trying to push anyone to the margins; we just want room to say what we believe without being shouted down.”

They say they back free speech for everybody, full stop, whatever someone’s orientation. “We’ll put our views on the table and we expect others to do the same,” Smith added. “That’s how a healthy society works.”

To make it clear they’re not staging a one-sided protest, they’re reaching out to LGBTQ+ voices—asking some to speak and others simply to come and listen. The goal, they say, is a civil exchange, not a shouting match.

They know people won’t suddenly agree on everything, but they’re betting that conversation beats silence and that respect can travel in both directions.

In June 1940, the liner Lancastria was pressed into service for Operation Aerial, the frantic evacuation of British troops and civilians from France. No one kept an exact count as the desperate crowd surged up the gangways; later estimates ran from 6,000 to 9,000 souls—more than four times the ship’s peacetime limit of 2,200.

On the afternoon of the 17th, while anchored off Saint-Nazaire on the Bay of Biscay, Lancastria was spotted by a German reconnaissance plane. Within minutes, Junkers Ju 88 bombers dived through the RAF patrol. Three bombs slammed home, detonating the fuel bunkers. In eighteen minutes the great hull rolled on its side and sank, trapping thousands below.

The death toll was staggering. The government, anxious to shield wartime morale, imposed a news blackout; newspapers were told to report only 1,738 lost. Survivors and researchers now believe the true figure tops 4,000—some say 6,000—making it the deadliest maritime disaster in British history.

The hull still lies twelve miles offshore, an unmarked war grave. Campaigners continue to ask France to give the site formal protection, but the seabed remains open to the tides—and to memory.

The Port of Dover, the gateway for most of Britain’s freight, has quietly turned into one of the country’s busiest crime scenes. In the last ten years, arrests have quadrupled—up 381%—as smugglers, stowaways and drug runners try to slip through the UK’s busiest ferry terminal.

Freedom-of-Information figures show the offences are a mixed bag: cocaine hidden in lorry panels, cigarettes stuffed in spare wheels, people in the back of vans, plus the usual scrapes—drunken fights, broken windows, thefts from waiting trucks.

Most arrests are for immigration breaches. In 2020, officers stopped 200 people sneaking in; seven years earlier the number was only 32. Officers say the routes keep shifting, and every month brings a new method.

Drugs tell the same story: 27 trafficking arrests in 2013, 104 in 2020. The port has answered with sniffer dogs, heartbeat detectors and a new drone that can read a number-plate from half a mile.

Chief Inspector Bill Payne insists his team can cope. “Every arrest is proof the system works,” he told the BBC. “We share intel with Border Force and Kent Police 24/7; if you’re bringing contraband through Dover, we’ll find it.”

Outside experts warn that extra boots, dogs and scanners cost money, and budgets are tight. Without more cash, they say, the port could become a bottleneck for crime as well as traffic.

Court records show most cases end in convictions, and low-level nuisance—shoplifting, vandalism—has actually fallen while officers focus on the bigger fish.

Besides chasing criminals, the port police keep the traffic moving, waving lorries through when French customs computers crash and stepping in before tempers boil over. Their visibility alone, Payne argues, scares plenty of offenders away.

The jump in arrests, he insists, is less a sign Dover is falling apart and more a sign his officers are getting better at spotting trouble before it sails into Britain.

Nigerian officials say the freed girls were met by a State Security Service officer—the agency that handles intelligence and national security—and their return feels like a hard-won win against Boko Haram.

Yet the joy is laced with pain: there is still no word on the Chibok schoolgirls seized six years ago, the kidnapping that launched the worldwide #BringBackOurGirls movement.  
Scores of them remain missing, an open wound for their parents and for the nation. Abuja keeps promising “we’re working on it,” but no solid news of rescue has ever come.

After arriving in the capital, the newly released girls were questioned, checked by doctors, given counselling, and sent home to their families. For the Chibok parents, the waiting room is still dark.

Talks led by human-rights groups and successive Nigerian administrations have achieved little. Despite official claims of “degrading” Boko Haram, the sect keeps striking, and most of the Chibok girls are still somewhere in the bush.

Public patience is wearing thin; every fresh attack deepens the anger that government cannot crush the insurgency or bring the girls back. Their story has come to stand for every girl denied school and every woman discounted by both militants and the state.

Abducted in April 2014, the Chibok girls have become the face of a lost generation, a reminder of the war’s toll on women, and a question still unanswered: when, if ever, will they walk through their parents’ doors again?

After the Manchester and London attacks, the UK government rolled out tighter security at big public gatherings, and Download at Donington Park is no exception. This year festival-goers are met by armed officers, extra stewards, bag searches at the gates, patrol dogs overhead in helicopters and hi-viz patrols weaving between the campsites.

A Leicestershire Police spokesperson said: “We know rifles and search teams can feel intimidating, but there’s no specific threat; we just want everyone to get home safely after a great weekend.”

Organisers have trimmed the permitted-items list to basics, asked fans to arrive early for searches and keep their eyes open. Despite the queues, the mood in the fields is upbeat: most say they’d rather lose ten minutes in a line-up than risk anything worse.

The same ramped-up presence is mirrored at events across the country, proof that Britain is determined to keep live music loud, proud and safe.

Cystic fibrosis is a genetic, lifelong illness that keeps the lungs inflamed and steadily steals a person’s breath. A single faulty gene tells the body to churn out mucus that’s thick and sticky; it clogs the lungs, pancreas, and other places it shouldn’t. In the lungs, that goo blocks the airways and turns them into a breeding ground for bacteria. Repeated infections and flare-ups scar the fragile tissue, and, bit by bit, breathing becomes a struggle. A wet cough that won’t quit, bouts of pneumonia or bronchitis, wheezing, and getting winded from everyday tasks are everyday realities.

The damage doesn’t stop at the lungs. When mucus plugs the pancreas, digestive enzymes can’t reach food, so nutrients pass right through. Kids can’t put on weight, and adults battle constant fatigue. Over time, some people develop CF-related diabetes, liver trouble, or brittle bones.

There’s no cure—yet. Daily routines revolve inhaled drugs to thin the mucus, antibiotics to tame infections, chest physiotherapy to shake the lungs clear, and, for those who hit the wall, a chance at a new set of lungs. Research has already added decades to many lives, but the disease still cuts them short. The work to find better therapies—and, one day, a cure—has never felt more urgent.

Though the incident looked grim, doctors say the player won’t need surgery—he’ll just face a long spell on the sidelines while the bone knits back together.

It happened midway through the eagerly awaited derby. Sterling, stretching to keep the ball in play, mistimed his lunge and caught his teammate flush, snapping a bone and igniting fresh debate about how brutal the game can be.

The 27-year-old—club and name kept quiet—hit the turf clutching his leg. Physios sprinted on, applied an air-cast and stretchered him off for scans at the nearby hospital.

The good news filtered through quickly: no operation required, only rest and rehab. Relief washed over the bench and the stands; the player himself managed a pained thumbs-up as he disappeared down the tunnel.

Sterling, shaken, later messaged his teammate: “Never meant to hurt you, bro. Hope you’re back out here soon.” He posted the same apology online, reminding followers that even accidental clashes carry consequences.

The episode has pushed player welfare back into the spotlight. Injuries happen, but clubs are again being urged to make safety every bit as important as three points.

Without their sidelined teammate, the squad still aims to keep the season alive. Depth, they insist, is on their side, and the injured player told them from his hospital bed, “Go win the next ones—I’ll be the loudest fan in the stands.”

“I never pictured walking away from Exxon,” he told us. “After four decades it felt like family, and I assumed I’d retire there. But when the call came it stopped me in my tracks; it felt like a rare way to serve the country on the world stage.”

Tillerson admits the offer caught him off-guard. “My whole life has been oil fields and balance sheets, so a diplomatic brief was the last thing I expected. Still, the itch to serve has always been there, and I figured the skills might translate.”

He chuckles at the learning curve. “Corporate life is tidy—targets, quarters, shareholders. Politics is weather in tornado season: every move gets magnified. Marry that chaos to four decades of negotiations across eighty-odd countries and, well, you hope the toolbox is deep enough.”

Switching sectors, he says, flips the scoreboard. “In business the metric is profit; in government it’s the national interest, and that’s harder to spreadsheet. The stakes feel heavier when the shareholders are 330 million Americans.”

Asked about foreign policy, he keeps it simple: “Show up, listen, keep your word. Alliances aren’t built in conference rooms; they’re built in the repeated small moments that earn trust. Years of airport lounges and midnight contract talks probably taught me more diplomacy than I realized.”

By the end of the conversation it’s clear: the oilman turned diplomat is still adjusting to the spotlight, but he’s all-in. Whether the gamble pays off—for him and for the country—remains an open chapter.

They bossed the game but still couldn’t find a way through. Huddersfield hogged the ball, probing and prodding, yet the breakthrough wouldn’t come. Elias Kachunga came closest, racing clear only to roll his shot inches wide of the far post.

The second half followed the same script—one-way traffic, bodies forward, crosses raining in—until, at last, the dam burst on 68 minutes. Tommy Smith whipped in a teasing ball and Steve Mounié thundered a header that left the keeper rooted.

Level for barely ten minutes. A razor-sharp pass split the defence, the visiting striker took a tidy touch and slipped it past the onrushing keeper.

Back came Huddersfield, undented. With time almost up, Jonathan Hogg sniffed a loose ball 25 yards out, let fly and watched it scream into the top corner. Stadium erupted.

Final whistle: 2-1. A tale of squandered chances turned into a lesson in grit. The win nudged them up the table and sent the home fans packing with a story they’ll retell for years.

The approach came just days before an international Test. Two players—whose names haven’t been released—went straight to team manager Jaliya Jayasekera and Sri Lanka Cricket’s anti-corruption unit after the bookmaker dangled a thick envelope, promising cash if they “managed” the result.

“We looked into it overnight and have already passed every scrap of evidence to the ICC,” Jayasekera told reporters.

The governing body isn’t brushing it off. Alex Marshall, the ICC’s anti-corruption chief, said his team will “lock arms” with Sri Lankan investigators to chase every lead. “Anyone caught will face the full force of the code,” he warned.

Fixing scares have become cricket’s unwanted shadow. Three years ago Australia’s captain Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were sent home for sanding the ball in Cape Town; the fallout still stains the Baggy Green.

Sri Lanka, hoping to stay ahead of the cheats, recently passed a sports law that can jail fixers for a decade and empty their bank accounts. Jayasekera says the ministry and board will keep drilling players on red flags. “The crooks don’t sleep, but neither will we,” he insisted.

Because the case is open, the approached players remain anonymous. Officials admit the story is a punch in the gut for team spirit, but promise tighter checks and education so the game’s integrity isn’t traded for a quick buck.

Scala’s been with Fifa since 2012. A Zurich native, he’s become one of the most visible faces inside the organization, chairing the Audit and Compliance Committee and carrying the unenviable job of trying to clean house after the corruption scandals broke. Two years ago he also took a seat on the Ad-Hoc Electoral Committee, the independent body Fifa brought in to keep an eye on its own elections.

Infantino, who grew up in Brig, Valais, built a solid résumé long before he swapped UEFA’s general-secretary office for the top floor at Fifa. When he was elected president in 2016, many saw it as the clearest signal yet that the association was serious about turning the page.

So, with two Swiss-Italians now occupying the biggest offices, there’s reason to hope the famously strict Swiss approach to governance might rub off on world football. If the same rules, transparency and caution that govern Swiss banks and town-hall meetings find their way into Fifa, the restructuring could actually stick.

Still, a shared passport doesn’t mean shared priorities. Infantino talks endlessly about reform and restoring credibility; whether Scala and the rest of the electoral committee will back him when tough choices arise is an open question.

This isn’t the first time Swiss-Italians have landed influential roles in the global game, and their growing presence could shape how football is run for years. If the new leadership keeps pushing openness, accountability and good governance, their ascent might turn out to be exactly what Fifa needs.

Susan O’Brien QC, who chairs the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, set a cut-off of 17 December 2014 simply because that is where the remit stops. Everything the panel hears must have happened on or before that day; it keeps the work focused and stops it sprawling forever.

O’Brien stressed that the inquiry is not hunting a few bad apples. It wants the full picture: how children in care were harmed, and which schools, homes, councils or churches looked away. A firm end-date makes the avalanche of statements, files and memories easier to handle and lets teams track patterns instead of chasing every fresh allegation.

She still urged anyone who knows anything—survivors, former staff, even people who only heard rumours—to speak up. “Tell us,” she said. “Your story helps us map where the system cracked and how to weld it shut.” The final report, due once hearings finish, will not just name names; it will recommend concrete changes so the same failures cannot happen again.

England arrived brimming with confidence after stringing wins together and were hungry for another to tighten their grip on top spot.  

West Indies, inserted after losing the toss, wobbled straight away. In-form Hayley Matthews flicked Brunt to slip for 15 in the third over and, moments later, Sciver nipped out Britney Cooper for 9. Captain Stafanie Taylor once again showed why she’s rated among the best, digging in for a hard-fought 57, but she found no lasting company. Deandra Dottin and Chedean Nation, usually so reliable, came and went cheaply, and the tail folded in a heap.  

Hartley’s 4 for 24 ripped through the lower order, while Brunt added three—Taylor’s the biggest—to leave the hosts all out for 155. It looked a below-par total, yet on their own patch West Indies still hoped their bowlers could exploit familiar conditions and make England sweat.

When Google bought Nest, it wasn’t just snapping up a line of sleek gadgets—it was hiring Tony Fadell’s instincts. The man nicknamed “the godfather of the iPod” brought more than a résumé; he showed up with an uncanny feel for what everyday people want before they know it themselves, plus a designer’s obsession over every screw and bevel.

The real gem inside Nest’s brushed-steel shells was the learning engine. The thermostat and smoke alarm quietly studied how families lived—when they woke, when they left, when they cranked the heat—then adjusted themselves without anyone lifting a finger. At the time, that kind of on-device machine learning was still science fiction for most living-room tech, and it handed Google a living lab for the connected home.

Nest also came with hundreds of thousands of already-hooked households. Overnight, Google had a direct pipeline to real customers who might one day buy lights, locks, or laundry machines that talk to one another. Every click, schedule tweak, and temperature nudge fed a feedback loop the company could mine for the next must-have thing.

On top of that, Nest’s sensors were quietly logging how much energy people actually use. With that data, Google could help shave electricity bills and maybe even nudge entire neighborhoods toward greener habits—valuable currency in the race to own the Internet of Things.

So the $3.2-billion price tag wasn’t just for thermostats; it bought Google a visionary leader, a self-teaching platform, a ready-made customer channel, and a mountain of real-world data to power the next generation of planet-friendly gadgets.

They left the fuel pods right where Cumsons and Tullygeasy Roads meet—brimming with premium gas and diesel, wedged into the tall grass like forgotten road-maintenance gear. The crew had rehearsed this drop for weeks; they knew they had maybe five minutes if a dog-walker or an early-shift farmer wandered past.

Bob—everyone just called him that, though his real name was longer and duller—had pinned each pod’s exact spot on a GPS app that talked to satellites most people didn’t know existed. To anyone driving by, the pods looked like innocent green boxes: maybe cable junctions, maybe rain gauges. Punch in the coordinates, though, and they became invisible pit stops for the outlaw rally that would rip through the district at dawn.

Sunrise bled over the hills while they worked, wrapping the pods in scrim and netting until even the shadows matched the hedgerows. Birds argued in the thorn trees; no human voices, no slamming doors—just the soft crunch of boots on gravel and the hiss of zip-ties tightening.

When the last knot was tied, Bob gave a low whistle. The team melted back into the hedges, leaving the crossroads looking exactly as sleepy as before. Only the map in their heads had changed.

Drivers would need to recall those spots from memory—no phones, no notes, no petrol-station cameras. Every second saved at a secret tank could be the second that kept them ahead of the roadblocks and the drones.

The junction, usually notable only for its potholes, was now a silent teammate in a race that didn’t officially exist. Somewhere down the lane each operative could already hear the first distant engine notes, like distant thunder. The clock was running, the stakes were everything, and the only certainty was that someone, somewhere, was already looking for what they’d just hidden.

At 18, Thomas Buckett tumbled 57 metres from a balcony during a party at a mate’s place in Sydney. The fall shattered vertebrae and left doctors doubting he’d walk again.

He refused to accept the sentence. After several operations and months of gruelling rehab, feeling crept back into his legs and hope returned. Locals followed every small win, dropping off meals and cheering when he managed a wiggle of a toe.

Two years later he took his first unsteady steps—an emotional, tear-filled moment he still calls “pure magic.” Physio sessions were brutal: nights of phantom pain, plateaus that felt like failures, and the constant fear of slipping backwards. He kept showing up.

Once he could manage stairs, he began volunteering with spinal-injury charities, sharing raw, honest talks about depression, pain, and persistence. If his story could shorten someone else’s darkness, he figured the fall was worth something.

The accident also rewired his future: engineering textbooks were swapped for anatomy ones. Now in his third year of a physiotherapy degree at the University of Sydney, he sometimes leans on a cane when fatigue hits, but he’s usually the one cracking jokes and rallying classmates for beach swims.

Thomas Buckett’s journey is proof that broken bodies don’t have to mean broken spirits—an everyday reminder to the rest of us that resilience isn’t a gift, it’s a decision repeated daily.

1. Agony for Rochdale: Bottom-third Rochdale were convinced they’d snatched a priceless win when they nosed ahead with nine minutes left, only for Millwall to nick an equaliser in stoppage time. One point instead of three leaves the Dale staring at the drop zone.

2. Kelman’s halfway-line stunner: Southend may be having a nightmare year, but Charlie Kelman lit it up by launching a 50-yard lob that sailed over the MK Dons keeper. Early contender for Goal of the Season? Absolutely.

3. Wigan’s Christmas cracker: Out-of-sorts Wigan stunned promotion-chasing West Brom 3-2 in a breathless game at the DW. The Latics’ faithful finally had something to sing about.

4. Forrest fires Pompey: Gavin Forrest rattled home a hat-trick as Portsmouth thumped Ipswich 4-1. A bright spot in an up-and-down Championship campaign for Pompey.

5. League Two’s record crowd: More than 15,000 braced the December chill for the Plymouth–Exeter derby and were rewarded with a feisty 1-1 draw and a new attendance benchmark for the division.

All told, the final round before the holidays served up the usual cocktail of gasps, groans and cheers, setting the table perfectly for the festive frenzy ahead.

After tearing it up for Kalmar, Antonsson’s phone wouldn’t stop buzzing; Leeds United won the race in August 2016, whisking him to England on a three-year deal and hoping his Swedish scoring form would jump the North Sea.

It didn’t quite work out that way. One season, three goals in 21 games, and suddenly the Yorkshire spotlight felt more like a glare. When competition stiffened the next year, he packed his bags for Blackburn Rovers on a season-long loan.

There, the net started rippling again—nine in 34 as Blackburn surged out of League One. Still, England didn’t make him an offer he couldn’t refuse, so in the summer of 2018 Antonsson headed home, signing with Malmö FF.

Back on familiar turf he looked like the player everyone remembered, banging in 16 in 30 during his first campaign and pushing Malmö into the title fight year after year. By 2020 he was among the Allsvenskan’s deadliest finishers, valued as much for his clever movement as his cold-blooded finishing. From Halmstads to Leeds, Blackburn to Malmö, he’s shown he can adapt, bounce back, and—most importantly—keep putting the ball in the net, something he plans on doing for a while yet.

Her family shared a heartfelt message with fans around the world: “With deep sorrow we say goodbye to our cherished mother, sister, grandmother, and great-grandmother, who slipped away after a long struggle with a rare dementia. We are devastated; everyone who loved her feels this ache.”

Carr’s résumé stretched more than fifty years, stacked with scene-stealing turns on Broadway and in film. Critics praised her ferocity, discipline, and old-school stage magic; audiences simply remembered the goose bumps she delivered.

Raised in New York, she started acting in the early ’60s and soon became the player directors called when they needed someone who could disappear into any skin. Hollywood beckoned, but she never gave up the boards, circling back to theater between pictures and collecting armfuls of awards for roles that ranged from glittering musicals to bruising dramas.

A few years ago Carr was diagnosed with an unusual strain of dementia. She kept the news quiet, leaning on family, and kept working as long as her body let her, turning up to set with script in hand and that trademark sparkle in her eye.

Her films and plays remain, but the woman who breathed life into them is gone. Colleagues, friends, and fans have flooded social media with memories. The family, asking for space to grieve, says a memorial will be announced later.

Police and volunteers have spent days combing the neighbourhood for any sign of Keith, who was reported missing by his worried family.

Keith is about 5’8”, with short grey hair and glasses. When he disappeared he was wearing a blue collared shirt, dark jeans and black shoes. His loved ones say he’s a regular in the local parks and never misses a chance to watch the birds.

The hashtag #FindKeith is now all over social media, shared by locals and strangers alike. Officers have also put out a public appeal. Sergeant James Howard, leading the search, said: “We’re deeply concerned for Keith. If you’ve seen him or know where he might be, please call us.”

A special helpline is open round the clock. Keith’s daughter, Rachel, added: “Dad is gentle and kind; he’d be heartbroken to know we’re suffering like this. Please help bring him home.”

Neighbours have joined forces with search teams, focusing on the parks Keith loved for birdwatching. Anyone with information, dash-cam or CCTV footage from the day he vanished is asked to ring the helpline or contact the police.

The Davies family and the whole community are holding onto hope that Keith will be found safe.

Kicking off the back half of the countdown, All Time Low team up with blackbear on “Monsters,” a pop-punk earworm that reminded everyone the Baltimore crew still had plenty of bite.

Billie Eilish saunters in at 19 with “Therefore I Am”—a snarky, self-owned anthem that felt like the perfect clap-back to 2020.

Taylor Swift surprised us all this year, and “Cardigan” (18) became the soft-focus centerpiece of her cottage-core detour, *Folklore*.

Tash Sultana’s “Pretty Lady” lands at 17; the one-woman loop-station wizard turns a breezy groove into a global sing-along.

HAIM slide into 16 with “The Steps,” a shrug-and-shred ode to outgrowing someone who can’t keep up.

AJR’s “Bang!” (15) pairs stadium-sized hooks with a quarter-life crisis—pure cathartic confetti.

Twenty One Pilots wrote “Level of Concern” (14) while the world locked its doors, turning anxiety into a danceable lifeline.

Glass Animals’ “Heat Waves” glides in at 13, all shimmering melancholy and late-night city shimmer.

Marcus Mumford strips it back for 12 with “Lay Your Head on Me,” a lullaby big enough for grown-up heartache.

Cannons close out this segment at 11; “Fire for You” smolders like a neon dream you can’t shake.

Stick around—your top 10 is up next.

Roedd y ddau ddyn yn aelodau o 1af Ffatwn, The Royal Tank Regiment, a chawsant eu hunain yn rhan o hyfforddiant ar faes yng ngogledd Sir Benfro. Roedd y ddau gorporal yn brofiadol ac yn gosod esiampl i bawb o'u cwmpas, gan ddangos y cyfrifoldeb a'r ymddygiad y disgwylid iddynt eu dangos.  

Bydd eu colli yn ergyd fawr i'r Fyddin Brenhinol, ac yn sioc i aelodau'r uned a'u teuluoedd sy'n galaru'n ddwys amdanyn nhw. Yn lle trefnu sesiynau adferiad grŵp, mae'r fyddin wedi dewis cyfnod o dawelwch a chefnogaeth unigol, gan gynnwys cwnsela a chymorth ymarferol i'r rhai sy'n trafod eu profedigaeth.  

Byddwn yn cofio Corporal Matthew Hatfield a Corporal Darren Neilson am eu hymrwymiad llwyr i'w gwaith ac i wasanaethu eu gwlad. Byddant yn parhau i gael eu cofio gyda pharch a chariad, ac yn parhau i ysbrydoli'r rhai sy'n dilyn eu hôl.  

Gyda llawer o dristwch a pharch, mae'r Fyddin Brenhinol a'r gymuned ehangach yn cyhoeddi bod gwasanaeth coffa i'r ddau wedi'i drefnu. Bydd yn gyfle i'r rhai a gafodd eu heffeithio gan eu colli ddod at ei gilydd, i gofio eu bywydau a'u gwasanaeth.  

Mae ymchwiliad i'r digwyddiad yn mynd rhagddo, gyda'r nod o ddysgu sut i osgoi sefyllfaoedd tebyg yn y dyfodol. Mae arweinyddiaeth y fyddin yn ailadrodd eu hymrwymiad i ddiogelwch a lles eu milwyr, a byddant yn gwneud popeth o fewn eu gallu i sicrhau hynny.

Moore, 33, has been hit with a string of driving charges that could land him in serious trouble.  

Police stopped him at a routine checkpoint in Waterside late one evening after spotting his Tamworth Proton Persona without a tax disc. A closer look revealed he also had no insurance, no L-plates, and—crucially—no qualified driver beside him, even though he’s still on a provisional licence. Officers thought they smelled drink on his breath, but the breathalyser came back inconclusive, so no alcohol-related charge was added.

He was arrested on the spot and later formally charged.

In court, solicitor John O'Donovan explained that Moore had been going through a rough financial patch and simply couldn’t afford to tax or insure the car. He stressed that his client was “genuinely sorry” and ready to accept whatever punishment the court imposes.

Judge Joanna McHugh acknowledged Moore’s remorse but reminded everyone that the rules are there to keep the roads safe. She adjourned sentencing until next month, warning that heavy fines and a licence suspension are likely. Moore was also urged to start working toward a full licence.

The case is a sharp reminder: skip the paperwork and the plates and the costs—financial and legal—quickly stack up.

Spain never loosened their grip on the game, turning their home patch into a private stage. Sergio Ramos strolled through the night like he owned it, stepping out of the back line to start attacks and still snapping every loose ball away. When a knock left him grimacing, he simply waved the physio aside—no way the captain was leaving this one early.

Andrés Iniesta conducted the middle third as if he had the ball on remote control. One velvet pass after another slit open the defence, and when the visitors tried to press, he disappeared them with a half-turn and a wink. You could almost see their midfielders’ shoulders sag.

David Silva spent the evening collecting bruises—opponents took turns to bump, tug and trip him—but every time he peeled himself off the turf he found another pocket of space. Looping balls over the top and low crosses skidding across the six-yard box kept the keeper busy and the scoreboard ticking.

Then came the moment no one in Alicante will need to describe twice. Villarreal’s Mario Gaspar flung himself skyward, back to goal, and connected with an overhead kick that hung in the air before ripping the net. The stadium gasped, roared, then settled into a long, appreciative hum; even the away end couldn’t help but clap.

Spain kept knocking but couldn’t add a fifth; two shots whistled inches wide and the crowd held its breath. No matter—the whistle confirmed another statement win for Vicente del Bosque’s side, polished off by Gaspar’s contender for goal of the year.

The players saluted every stand before disappearing down the tunnel, applause raining down like confetti. Del Bosque, grinning like a proud grandfather, singled out Gaspar’s acrobatics and Ramos’ refusal to quit. Another night, another reminder why these are the European champions. The world already has the next date circled—if this is the standard, nobody wants to miss what comes next.

Ministers are growing anxious because the short-term rules that were slapped on Romania and Bulgaria when they joined the EU run out soon. Worried that a fresh wave of job-seekers could swamp schools, hospitals and the benefits office, the government wants to shut the door on some public services.

The old Freedom to Work rules, which capped how many Romanians and Bulgarians could settle and take jobs here, disappear on New Year’s Eve. After that, their citizens will have the same open-door rights as French or Polish newcomers.

Whitehall’s fear is that if thousands arrive at once and can claim housing help, tax credits or GP appointments from day one, the system will creak. So officials are sketching plans to delay or trim access to benefits, non-urgent NHS care and council homes for new arrivals.

Critics call the idea mean-spirited and possibly illegal, but ministers insist they’re simply guarding stretched services. They say help will still be there for people who truly need it, just not on tap the moment someone steps off the plane.

Under the draft rules, recent migrants would queue separately for social housing, wait longer for unemployment support, and be billed for some routine treatment. Emergency care and schooling would stay free.

Opposition parties, charities and church groups warn the policy could push families into bedsits, foodbanks and the black economy, hardening prejudice along the way. They want guarantees that no one ends up sleeping rough because the safety net has holes.

With only months to go, the argument is turning ugly. The Home Office has to square the right to work against the right not to wait six months for a doctor’s appointment. Supporters of the curb say it buys time for councils to build houses and train nurses; critics say it buys votes by stoking fear. Either way, the New Year is shaping up to be a flashpoint in the never-ending row over who gets what in modern Britain.

After weeks of late-night talks and arm-wrestling, the bosses finally blinked: leagues can now set their own calendars. Purists scream that it’s a recipe for fixture mayhem, yet the European Professional Football Leagues insist the move will make the game hungrier from top to bottom.

An EPFL spokesman called it “a historic handshake with the game’s future. Leagues can finally pick kick-off times that suit their weather, their travel, their fans—no more one-size-fits-all Saturdays at three.”

But, he added, “freedom isn’t a free pass.” Empty stands and shredded hamstrings help nobody, so the EPFL will keep a watching brief on pile-ups and tired legs. “We’ll be on the phone with every league, the players’ union, the doctors—if the toll gets too high, we’ll step in.”

Analysts predict local derbies on Wednesday nights and derby days moved to suit TV prime time could lift ratings; others fret about clashes with World Cup qualifiers and burnout. The biggest fear is a free-for-all over the plum 8 p.m. slots.

Still, the EPFL is unmoved. “We trust the people who know their fans best. Give them the keys, and they’ll drive the game forward.”

Whatever unfolds, the calendar will never look the same, and fans across continents will feel the ripple—whether it’s a derby under Friday lights or a title race compressed into a breathless final fortnight.

After months of rumors and back-room talks, Torquay United supporters finally got the news they’ve been waiting for: Gaming International is buying the club. Word came down on Tuesday that the deal is done, and Plainmoor is already buzzing.

Gaming International—GI to most—is a Swindon-based gaming and leisure outfit that’s been circling football for years. Buying the Gulls is their first real plunge into the pro game, and they’re keeping the price tag quiet for now.

Clifford Baker, GI’s CEO, can’t hide his grin: “We’re thrilled to bring the Gulls into the family. The club’s got history, heart and a set of fans who live and breathe every kick—that’s exactly what we want to build on.”

He promises more than cash. “We’ll back the squad, but just as important we’ll invest in the town—better community work, smarter fan experiences, and a youth setup that keeps talent coming through.”

Founded in 1899, Torquay have spent most of their life bobbing between the divisions, lately stuck in the National League doldrums. Supporters hope new money and know-how can nudge them upward again.

Online forums and the terraces are already day-dreaming about promotion; most fans figure anything beats the roller-coaster of recent seasons.

Over the next fortnight the old and new regimes will huddle on budgets, staff and a shared vision so match-day life feels seamless when pre-season starts.

In short, the Gulls have a fresh owner, a fresh wallet and a fresh shot at glory. Next season could be the start of something special—or another chapter of “what if.” Either way, the yellow-and-blue choir will be there, singing the lads on and praying the tide has finally turned.

This is a milestone day in Wales: the four future-generations commissioners are sitting down together—in public, at City Hall—for an open, unscripted conversation. For the first time, children, older residents, Welsh-language communities and tomorrow’s yet-unborn citizens will have their champions around one table.

Each commissioner speaks for a different slice of Welsh life, so the chat will wander across the worries and hopes they carry—from playground rights to pensioner dignity, from keeping Welsh alive to keeping the planet liveable. Their stories overlap: how climate, Covid, poverty, language and education collide in real lives.

The session is designed to be a two-way street. Anyone can turn up, listen and put a question. The aim is not another report but a shared brainstorm on the practical next steps for a fairer, greener, bilingual Wales.

Wales may be small, but this kind of cross-generation, cross-cultural huddle is rare anywhere. If it works, the format could travel—proof that divided communities can still question, learn and plan together.

People across the country have marked the date in their diaries, curious to see whether talking openly can nudge everyday life in a better direction.

The site lets anyone in the UK start or sign a petition about anything the government could actually change. Hit 10,000 names and Whitehall has to answer in public; hit 100,000 and Parliament can decide to debate it, so your gripe lands on the front bench instead of just your Facebook feed.

It’s the government’s own corner of the internet, built to look open rather than ominous: one green “start a petition” button, a short form, a few hints on gathering support, and a running list of what’s live, what’s closed, and what ministers said back.

Petitions still have to play by the rules—keep it clean, keep it within Westminster’s remit—and the moderators are quick to bin anything that strays. Beneath the hood, the “Parliament Debates” page stores every word spoken in the Commons when a petition forces the issue, so you can see if your campaign changed minds or merely minutes.

The whole thing is less revolution than invitation: a simple way for anyone with a postcode and a pulse to shove an idea under the nose of the people who can sign it into law.

This place is motor-racing legend. Over the years the tarmac has soaked up epic duels, last-lap miracles and some heart-stopping shunts. Plenty of riders have left their tyre prints here, yet only the fearless few have ever truly owned the lap record.

What makes the lap so special is the way it stitches together flat-out straights, hair-pin chicanes and climbs that yank your stomach into your throat—all while the old-town balconies watch on like grandstands. Gone are the gentle green verges; raw concrete walls now line the circuit, offering zero forgiveness and 100 % concentration tests.

Even the old hands treat every lap like defusing a bomb: hit the apex a metre late and you’re in the scenery; breathe on the throttle a millisecond early and the rear steps out. And just to keep everyone humble, the sky can flip from blazing sunshine to thick fog or a monsoon between morning warm-up and the chequered flag.

Out here raw speed is only half the story. The real trick is thinking faster than the bike can accelerate—picking a line, changing your mind, re-picking it, all before the next marker board flashes past. One botched decision through the snaking esses and the weekend’s work ends in the gravel.

While the rider gets the cheers, an invisible army keeps the show alive: spanner-turning mechanics, laptop-wielding strategists, calm-voiced psychologists, even the chef who times the pasta to the second—everyone chasing the same perfect Sunday.

When the visor snaps shut the world shrinks to a tunnel of sound: the motor howling at 14,000 rpm, gears banging like gunshots, and your own pulse hammering in your ears. Outside, the stands erupt; inside, it’s just you and the next corner rushing up at 200 km/h.

A blink costs tenths; a breath costs more. At these speeds the bike feels like it’s folding space, colours smearing into ribbons. Pain, fatigue, even the roar of the crowd vanish—only the racing line and the stopwatch still exist.

To survive you need the reflexes of a cat and the calm of a monk. There are no time-outs, no “next shift,” just an unbroken 25-minute knife fight with physics and your own doubts. Win, and you join the ghosts of giants; hesitate, and you become a cautionary tale. The flag drops once—make it count.

That’s 38 percent more than the same stretch last year, and it lines up with Donald Trump’s promise to supercharge ICE and squeeze “sanctuary cities” that won’t help with deportations.

But here’s the thing: most of the people swept up don’t have criminal records. Earlier this year, arrests of non-criminals more than doubled, topping 10,800.

The spike feels like a living snapshot of the administration’s hard-line immigration policy. Agents are scooping up not only longtime residents with old, minor convictions but also neighbors who’ve never been in trouble with the law.

Even so, ICE arrests are still short of the 2014 peak under Barack Obama. If the pace holds, though, the agency is on track to blow past that record by December.

The raids have sent a shiver through immigrant neighborhoods. Advocacy groups warn the dragnet is sowing panic and tearing families apart.

Supporters counter that the law is finally being enforced. Anyone without papers, they say, is fair game for deportation—criminal history or not—and past administrations simply looked the other way.

For critics, the numbers show the net has widened far beyond “bad hombres.” As the country wrestles over what its immigration rules should be, the ripple effects from ICE’s new playbook are already reshaping communities from coast to coast.

The centre-back, famous for his straight-talking defending and natural captain’s presence, never managed to nail down a starting place at Leeds and was quietly ushered out after a single frustrating season. With Marcelo Bielsa overhauling the squad, the Championship club simply didn’t have space for the former Hearts skipper.

He clocked up 15 games in all competitions, none ending with his name on the scoresheet. Crossing the border had looked like a career boost; instead it fizzled out after an earlier trial at Rangers had already fallen flat.

His release set tongues wagging back in Scotland. A romantic return to Tynecastle was mooted, but Craig Levein has cooled that talk, suggesting the 28-year-old will have to plot his next move elsewhere.

Still, the defender is adamant his story is far from finished. His agent insists: “He’s got plenty left at the top level and will show it next season, wherever that may be.”

Between his Scottish know-how and dressing-room influence, suitors are already circling. The only question now is whether his future lies in the Premiership or further afield.

To make sure every young person gets top-notch support, the organization will roll out a tough, must-pass certification for everyone who works with youth—mentors, tutors, job coaches, the lot. The test will look at what they know, what they can do, and how well they connect with kids in real life.

This isn’t a “one and done” deal; certificates will be renewed every few years so staff stay sharp as roles shift, research moves on, and young people’s needs evolve.

On top of that, a clear, practical code of ethics will spell out how adults should behave with the kids and families they serve—think honesty, respect, and airtight confidentiality.

If someone slips up, the body can investigate complaints and, if needed, hand out warnings, suspend, or fully pull a worker’s certification to keep young people safe.

It will also keep the workforce growing by running free or low-cost trainings, workshops, and seminars that share the newest findings and best tricks of the trade.

By keeping a close eye on standards, the organization plans to lift the whole sector, so youth programs and work-based learning deliver better results for kids and their families.

Adult diapers have been a lifeline for millions—older adults, people with disabilities, anyone coping with incontinence—yet the product itself is stuck in the 1950s. For almost eighty years the basic blueprint hasn’t changed, and that, says Anita Fader, is a quiet scandal. “We’ve settled for ‘good enough’ instead of asking what these products should actually do for the people who depend on them.”

Fader, a continence-tech researcher at the University of Southampton, is tired of waiting. Yes, today’s diapers swap in super-absorbent powders and smell-blocking beads, but the core idea—wrap the user in a bulky, plastic-backed shell—remains the same. The result is familiar to anyone who’s worn or changed one: heat rash, chafing, the tell-tale bulge under clothes, and the constant worry that someone might notice.

Her lab is starting from scratch. By weaving in breathable textiles, stretch circuits and low-profile sensors, they’re building prototypes that look and feel like normal underwear yet can text a caregiver the moment they’re wet. The aim isn’t a gentler tweak; it’s a dignity-restoring leap that makes incontinence one more manageable part of life instead of the part that defines it. To get there, engineers, material scientists and—crucially—users who live with leaks every day are designing together, turning embarrassment into empowerment.

Ireland and Northern Ireland have rolled out a joint plan to wrestle down the mountain of debt that’s been piling up on households, firms and the public purse.

Step one is a clean-up of the banks’ books: officials are hunting for every “non-performing” loan—the ones people or companies haven’t touched in months—and packaging them for sale to specialist investors. Off-loading these toxic loans gives lenders room to start lending again.

At the same time, regulators on both sides of the border have tightened the rules on new credit. Banks now face stiffer stress tests, tighter underwriting and a sterner lecture on responsible lending so the next wave of defaults never materialises.

For loans already on the books, many banks have opened “restructure desks”: rates can be shaved, terms stretched, or part of the balance simply written off if the borrower can show genuine hardship.

Northern Ireland is also coordinating with Westminster to make sure Brexit-related trade hiccups don’t push more firms over the edge, while Dublin is preparing a personal-insolvency regime that could give families breathing space—and even wipe a slice of what they owe.

None of this is simple. Selling debt to vulture funds can feel like shifting the mess into someone else’s garden, and every tweak has to be walked through a minefield of legal, political and market risk. Officials admit the playbook will need constant rewrites as the post-COVID economy keeps throwing curveballs.

Even after the way it ended, the gaffer still believes his best days in football are ahead. Oldham finished 17th, only seven points off the drop, but that thin margin told the story of a season that never caught light.

Chairman Simon Corney admitted the parting hurt. “We’re grateful for everything he’s done,” Corney said, “but the club needs a fresh voice if we’re going to climb away from danger. Staying in League One is the minimum; pushing upwards is the aim.”

The former boss, once a ferocious midfielder, took flak from every angle—supporters, radio phone-ins, even former teammates questioned his line-ups. He shrugged it off, pointing to a skeleton squad and a calendar that looked like rush-hour traffic.

Still, the sack stung. “Managing is all I’ve ever wanted,” he said the morning after clearing his desk. “I’ve banked lessons you can’t buy. The next club will get a better version of me.”

Around Oldham and beyond, pub debates rage on: was he doomed from day one, or simply never given time to lay real foundations?

For now he’ll skip the dug-out, recharge, watch games as a fan again. But he’s already scribbling ideas in a notebook, convinced the story doesn’t finish here.

Oldham, meanwhile, have drawn up a shortlist and started interviews. They need someone who can turn “must-win” into actual wins—starting with the first whistle of pre-season.

The summer transfer window is where next season’s story starts getting written. A couple of smart signings in July can rescue a club that limped over the line in May, while a dud window can poison the whole year.

Clubs spend these weeks hunting for any edge: marquee names to sell shirts, hidden gems to flip later, or deadwood to shift so the wage bill breathes again. Every deal is a chance to rebalance the squad before the opener.

When a dressing-room general leaves, replacing him isn’t just desirable—it’s urgent. Leave a hole unfilled and tactics collapse, egos wobble, and points slip away before the leaves turn.

For boards sweating over spreadsheets, the window is also the annual cash register. One big sale or a handful of loans can keep the lights on and the accountants quiet.

Momentum is set here too. Fans arrive at the first game either buzzing about the new number nine or groaning at the lack of one, and players feel the difference. A single thrilling arrival can lift a whole dressing room; a failed chase can sap it.

So the summer window isn’t just paperwork and medicals—it’s the stretch of weeks that quietly decides whether a club spends the next nine months dreaming of Europe or looking over its shoulder at the drop zone.

The crowd trickles in under a sky so blue it could be a postcard, the kind of midwestern blue that makes everything feel bigger than it is. Vans with satellite dishes on top nose into the grass, and young staffers in campaign tees weave through the rows, clutching clipboards and coffee, grinning like they’ve already won. Overhead, banners snap in the breeze, the bald eagle printed on them looking fierce enough to swoop down and start job-interviewing people on the spot.

Then Mitt Romney appears, sleeves rolled just enough to say “I’m ready to work,” and the cheers roll across the field like thunder. He’s done this a thousand times—handshake, smile, steady eye contact—so the whole thing feels less like a performance and more like muscle memory. His navy suit never wrinkles; the flag-striped scarves around him flutter like they rehearsed it.

Every sign, every bumper sticker, every speaker who warms up the mic keeps landing on the same word: jobs. “Jobs, not taxes.” “More work, less welfare.” The phrase gets chanted, sung, printed in block letters until it’s stuck in your head like a pop chorus.

Ohio, hosting the show, knows the lyrics by heart. This used to be the place that put the world on wheels, and now it’s trying to figure out how to keep its kids from leaving for Austin or Asheville. Empty plants loom on the edge of town like concrete ghosts, but today the stage backdrop shows men in hard hats bending steel under a sunrise that never happens on the third shift. It’s nostalgia packaged as promise.

So Romney, framed against that painted skyline, talks about spreadsheets and start-ups, about bringing the hustle of Palo Alto to the assembly lines that once built Buicks. He doesn’t say “rust belt” out loud; he says “renewal.” The crowd roars anyway, because hope—especially the jobs-flavored kind—still tastes pretty good out here.

These extra trophies shine a light on the sweat and heart players, coaches, and teams poured into the game over the last twelve months. Here’s what’s up for grabs:

1. African Club of the Year – goes to the continent’s top side that mixed trophies with fearless football and kept getting better every week.  
2. African Coach of the Year – for the tactician whose game plans turned a team (or a rising star) into a story we couldn’t stop talking about.  
3. Most Promising Talent of the Year – a tip of the cap to the teenager who already looks like tomorrow’s headline act.  
4. Goal of the Year – the strike that made us jump off the couch, a mix of audacity and pure technique.  
5. Fair Play Award – for the player or squad that reminded us respect is still part of the sport, even when the stakes are sky-high.  
6. African Referee of the Year – the whistle-blower who kept the game honest, calm, and flowing when tempers threatened to boil.  
7. African Women’s Player of the Year – the continent’s queen of the pitch, plain and simple.  
8. African Women’s National Team of the Year – the side that turned teamwork into silverware and inspired a new wave of girls to lace up boots.

A panel of seasoned African-football minds will vote after weighing every nominee’s year-long body of work. Come awards night, we’ll toast the talent that keeps the continent’s beautiful game alive and kicking.

They were in two separate cars when everything went wrong. Rhodri Miller had the wheel of a black VW Golf; Alesha O’Connor and Corey Price were riding with him. Margaret Challis was alone in her green VW Polo. Just after dark on Friday, 6 March 2015, their paths crossed in the worst way.

Police say the young friends had been part of a line of cars “racing” and swerving along the A470 past Storey Arms. Speed sent Rhodri’s car into oncoming traffic; the impact killed them all.

The news hollowed out two valleys. Barry Comprehensive, where Rhodri and Corey were in Year 12, and St Richard Gwyn, where Alesha studied, felt like different places on the Monday morning that followed. Teachers spoke to half-empty classrooms; corridors that usually echoed with laughter fell quiet.

Margaret’s family lost a nanna who still collected her neighbours’ parcels and baked for church sales. Friends of the teenagers kept replaying the last Snapchat, the last joke, the last wave through a car window.

In the aftermath, parents, councillors and police pressed for better driver education. Schools brought in hard-hitting talks; local councils backed “Safe Drive, Stay Alive” sessions. Fund-raisers followed—five-a-side tournaments, cake stalls, a charity head-shave—every penny to road-safety charities. Each March, lanterns are lit on the hillside above the crash site: four points of light for Alesha, Rhodri, Corey and Margaret, and a quiet promise to take the next bend that little bit slower.

Losing Johnny Sexton is a hammer-blow for Leinster; the man who pulls the strings could be out for months, and the attack suddenly looks rudderless.

The club still hasn’t spelled out the damage, but word is he took an awkward fall on his shoulder in Saturday’s final and walked off cradling it in agony.

The defeat itself stings just as much. favourites Leinster were out-fought by a relentless Connacht, and while Sexton’s early exit didn’t help, it shouldn’t overshadow the victors’ brilliant display.

Confirmation that the fly-half needs surgery darkens Leinster’s off-season. With 70-plus caps for Ireland, Sexton is more than first-choice; he’s the heartbeat of the squad. Replacing that influence is a monumental task.

“We’re gutted for Johnny,” head coach Leo Cullen said. “Surgery is unavoidable, so now it’s all about supporting his rehab.”

No timeline has been given, but Leinster must already map out life without him. A temporary No. 10 is essential for pre-season, whether from inside the camp or the market.

Ross Byrne has filled in before, while younger brother Harry is waiting for a real shot. Still, the province could still shop for a seasoned general to steady the ship.

Across the province, fans are sending speedy-recovery wishes. Sexton is cherished for last-ditch drop goals and last-ditch tackles alike, and his absence will echo well beyond the scoreboard.

They were convinced that chunks of the wreck were still locked in the peat, the kind of soft, treacherous bog that blankets much of Ireland. With old logbooks, stories from farmers who’d watched the sky that night, and the newest lidar and magnetometry kit, they set out to bring the rest of the aircraft back into the light.

It wasn’t wishful thinking. Ever since the Army swept through in ’43, locals had been turning up shards of aluminum while cutting turf. Each glint in the spade meant something bigger might still be down there, slowly sinking.

They rented a scruffy house on the edge of the village and started walking the bog in tight lines. Week after week they cut slices of peat no wider than a dinner plate, ran detectors over the spoil, and watched the radargrams for hard shapes beneath the moss. When the rain came—and it always came—they worked under plastic sheeting that snapped like a flag in the Atlantic wind.

The bog fought back. Roots as thick as wrists clogged the shovels; the wet peat tried to suck boots off legs. Still, they kept going, sustained by thermoses of tea and the thought that somewhere below, the rest of the plane was waiting.

Then the detector squealed. Forty centimetres down they struck corrugated metal, painted olive drab. Careful brushing revealed a six-foot section of fuselage skin still riveted to a frame. Nearby they uncovered engine cowling, a fragment of wing spar, and, heartbreakingly, a scorched leather flying glove with the owner’s name inked inside.

They lifted everything in numbered trays, photographed, bagged, and drove it to the conservation lab. Months later the pieces went on display in the county museum under low lights, quiet witnesses to a story that had almost been swallowed by the earth.

The dig taught them more than history. Marrying high-tech surveys with the slow craft of trowel and brush, they proved it was still possible to coax lost relics out of Ireland’s bogs. Other teams now copy the method, chasing everything from Viking longboats to downed WWII fighters.

New projects have taken the crew to every corner of the country, but on wet nights they still talk about the bog that gave up its secret, reminding them that the past isn’t gone—it’s just waiting for someone stubborn enough to keep digging.

The FA has charged Chelsea midfielder Mikel Obi after he stormed into referee Mark Clattenburg’s dressing room following the club’s stormy 3-2 home loss to Manchester United on 28 October.

Officials say Mikel used threatening and abusive language; if proven, he faces a heavy fine and a possible ban. Friends claim the Nigerian was incensed by suggestions Clattenburg racially abused him during the match—allegations the referee flatly denies.

The player hasn’t contested the charge but has asked to plead his case in person, while Chelsea insist he reacted to “unacceptable racial language.” The FA, working alongside the Met Police, has paused its own probe so the criminal investigation can proceed unhindered.

A guilty verdict could land Mikel a suspension of up to eight games under recent disciplinary precedents for violent or threatening conduct.

The episode deepens a chaotic campaign for Chelsea, already rocked by boardroom upheaval and on-field slides. Mikel, a mainstay since 2006 with 300-plus club appearances, would leave a sizeable gap if sidelined; the final fallout, however, rests on the FA’s eventual ruling.

Kinlochshiel just kept rolling. Week after week they banked another single point, and somehow that was enough to stay clear at the summit. Every win felt routine, yet each one still felt like a shot of confidence straight to the veins.

The secret sauce? A game plan that morphed to fit whoever stood in the opposite dug-out, plus a squad that genuinely enjoyed passing to each other. Their coach, a quiet man with a magician’s eye for shape, would tweak one hinge and the whole machine clicked tighter.

Every shirt mattered. The back line turned half-chances into throw-ins, the midfield treated the ball like a private joke no opponent could understand, and the forwards kept cashing in, pinging the net and keeping the scoreboard—and the table—on their side.

Early doors, nobody had them pegged for anything except a relegation scrap. They’d stuttered, dropped points, shipped soft goals. Instead of folding, they took it personally, trained harder, and turned the season into a slow-burn revenge tour.

Soon the terraces were packed, scarves twirling, voices cracking. Being the surprise package made them everyone’s second team, and the roar that greeted every clearance or clever turn felt like an extra substitute.

Pressure grew, but Kinlochshiel treated it like background noise. They still chased that single point every Saturday, and every time it landed, belief climbed another notch.

There were wobbles—last-gasp tackles, late free-kicks, games that felt like staring contests—but they always found the spare yard or the clever foul, nicking the draw that felt like a win. The gap inched wider.

When the final whistle blew on the campaign, they were still top. Champions. The team that “came from nowhere” had been right here all along, stacking points, trusting the process, and proving that grit, unity and a clever plan can turn underdogs into the ones holding the trophy at the end.

After months of rumors, the 21-year-old has finally put pen to paper for Sunderland AFC, linking up again with his old boss David Moyes. He still credits Moyes for handing him his Premier League debut and insists that first taste of top-flight football set the tone for everything that followed.

He’ll also be rejoining Donald Love and Paddy McNair, who moved to the Stadium of Light earlier in the window for a joint fee hovering around £5 million. The three came through the Manchester United ranks under Moyes and know each other’s game so well that Sunderland’s hierarchy saw the reunion as a no-brainer.

Supporters greeted the announcement with a roar of approval; they’re desperate for a spark after a stuttering start to the campaign and believe the youngster’s energy in midfield is exactly what’s been missing. 

Moyes beamed at his unveiling: “His range of passing, vision and that drive from deep can pull us up the pitch. I’ve always believed in him—now I get to prove why.”

The deal also sends a message that, despite the club’s well-documented cash headaches, Sunderland are serious about climbing the table. The board are sticking with Moyes, convinced a manager with his CV will come good once the pieces fall into place.

Throw in the familiarity of Love and McNair, and suddenly the Black Cats look like a squad trying to turn the page on recent gloom and chase the glory days of old. For the 21-year-old, it’s a stage set for him to lock down a Premier League future and show the wider world what all the fuss is about.

France is moving to shut down the Revolutionary Nationalist Youth after a spate of street fights culminated in the death of a 19-year-old left-wing protester. Known by its French initials JNR, the group is a far-right outfit whose supporters flaunt swastika tattoos and have been blamed for a string of clashes with leftist activists.

Investigators are now tracing ties between the JNR and similar movements across Europe, part of a wider push to keep violent fringe groups from gaining ground. Officials say years of flat wages, immigration rows and general fed-up-ness have turned extremist rhetoric into a growth industry.

Interior Minister Manuel Valls will put the break-up order before the cabinet this week. Only the president can sign off on a ban, but every security and judicial voice in the country will be heard first. If the decree goes through, the JNR’s name, logo and bank accounts vanish overnight; even wearing one of their T-shirts could land you in court.

Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault left no room for doubt: “Groups that preach violence and trample the Republic have no place here.”

JNR boss Serge Ayoub shot back that his boys are being framed, yet a video circulating online catches him urging followers to “crack lefty skulls.” Police also suspect the JNR left a student fighting for his life after a melee last spring.

The timing matters: with the far right polling higher each year, officials hope dissolving the JNR will send a warning that the line between angry speech and blood on the pavement will cost you your organization.

When he stepped in for Ashley Hoskin back in October 2015, the ex-Chesterfield first-team coach didn’t just inherit a squad—he took on a project. Drawing on the know-how that had revived Chesterfield, he rolled out new systems almost overnight, preaching shape, tempo, and belief.

The opening months were rocky: long treatment-room queues, a run of brutal fixtures, and a table that made grim reading. Yet he stayed calm, patched holes with academy kids, tweaked formations mid-game, and somehow kept picking up points. Between matches he was on the road scouting Sunday-league parks and League Two reserves, turning up gems and coaxing more from the ones already there.

Training grew louder and sharper. Instead of barking orders, he pulled players aside, showed them clips of their own good moments, and said, “Do that for ninety minutes.” Laughter returned to the canteen; results followed on the pitch. Win after win nudged them up the league, and what had felt like a relegation fight began to look like a promotion push.

The dressing-room trusted him because he trusted them first. They swore by his small-sided games, the Friday morning “free-role” experiments, the way he ended every session by gathering everyone in a huddle and asking, “Who’s going to make the difference tomorrow?”

Season by season the graph only pointed up. The club, once sleep-walking, woke up to new stands, new songs, and a new expectation: that every year they should be in the mix. And at the heart of it was the quiet man from Chesterfield who had simply come in, done the basics brilliantly, and reminded everyone what pride felt like.

Gillian first met Rachel and Nyomi at a neighborhood book club ages ago.  
They clicked over dog-eared paperbacks, the perfect cup of coffee, and the collective belief that odd-looking cats are superior cats.  
What started as chats about plot twists drifted into real life—kids, jobs, heartbreaks—until the three of them felt more like family than friends.

When Rachel’s son Liam arrived, Gillian became the honorary aunt: rocking him through teething nights, learning the difference between a hungry cry and a tired one, buying tiny sneakers he’d outgrow in a month.  
Liam’s laugh bounced off the thin townhouse walls so often it became their soundtrack.

Then the calls went unanswered.  
Coffee dates were “forgotten.”  
Gillian’s offers to babysit were met with tight smiles and quick excuses.  
Mutual friends whispered that the Fees were struggling, but no one said struggling with what.

The truth slammed into her one afternoon: bruises shaped like fingerprints on Liam’s arms, a flinch when she reached for a hug.  
She confronted them; screaming matches replaced movie nights.  
Doors slammed, phones blocked, the friendship cremated in real time.

Gillian called child services that same night.  
Paperwork, delays, more delays.  
Before anyone could act, the Fees vanished—rental truck gone before sunrise.

Two weeks later a small obituary appeared online.  
Liam, three years old.  
Gillian sat on the kitchen floor, phone still warm in her hand, unable to breathe.

She now speaks in school auditoriums and church basements, teaching strangers how to spot the quiet signs of abuse.  
Every slideshow, every pamphlet, is an apology to a little boy who laughed like wind chimes and to two friends she can’t stop loving or hating.

Ray, Tony, Mackey and their ringleader Eddie had been trawling the estates of Kirkcaldy for weeks, hunting for the perfect score. Word on the street was that small-time dealer Dwayne Kinner was sitting on more gear than he could shift in a year.

They picked a night when the frost bit hard and the streets were empty. For three days they’d watched the house, clocking who came and went, and by midnight they were sure only Dwayne and his cousin Nicholas were inside.

They slipped in through the back door. Tony and Mackey crept toward the kitchen while Ray followed Eddie up the stairs. The telly was blaring; the pair were glued to a game. The rest of the terrace seemed to hold its breath.

“Talk, Dwayne,” Eddie growled, gun raised. “We know you’re holding. Where’s it kept?”

Dwayne paused the game, unhurried. “And why would I tell you that?”

Downstairs, cupboards flew open, drawers clattered. Nothing. Either their snitch had lied or Dwayne had moved it. Tony’s whispered swearing drifted up the stairwell.
