They herded the cousins into the living room, two pistols now trained on them.

“Thought it would be smash-and-grab, did you?” Dwayne taunted. “Burst in, grab my wages, stroll off into the night?”

Eddie jabbed the barrel against Dwayne’s temple. “Don’t try me…”

Then everything flipped. Nicholas, quiet until now, hurled himself at Mackey, twisted the machete free and sprang up swinging. Dwayne rammed an elbow into Eddie’s ribs, slipped his grip and bolted for the back door.

What was meant to be an easy robbery became a scramble to stay alive. The hunters were suddenly the prey, and in that frozen second they realised their plan hadn’t just collapsed—it had blown up in their faces.

Inside Notre-Dame the air felt heavy, yet electric: grief pressed down, but something stubborn rose to meet it. When the old bells began their slow toll, no one spoke; the sound alone carried the names of those who were gone.

President Hollande stepped forward, pale and plainly exhausted. His voice bounced off stone that had survived revolution, occupation, fire. “We are cracked,” he said, “not broken. We mourn, and then we stand—together.” The sentence was simple, almost whispered, but it landed like an order.

In the pews survivors balanced on canes and folded into scarves, eyes fixed ahead. Their bodies still carried the night of the attacks—some in wheelchairs, some with hearing aids that squeaked when they hugged—but they came, because showing up felt like the first answer to terror.

Beside them, parents, partners, children clutched photographs worn soft by handling. Tears slipped silently; no one bothered to wipe them away. Every so often a hand reached across the aisle and found another hand. Strangers or not, it didn’t matter—permission to grow roots for a minute or two.

Outside, Paris kept breathing, but inside the cathedral the country took stock: broken, yes, and still insistently alive. When the bells finally quieted and the organ let out its last breath, people filed onto the parvis slower than they’d arrived, coats drawn tight against a cold they suddenly felt. They left carrying the same weight, but they left side by side, which, for tonight, was enough.

Lucas refused to let one bad race write his story. After stalling at the start line, he shrugged off the embarrassment and told himself, “That wasn’t me.”

The wins that followed didn’t come easy. Every track threw a fresh curve—new hills, tighter turns, cocky kids who’d grown up on two wheels. Lucas answered with lungs that wouldn’t quit and a head that never dropped. If someone shot ahead, he kept the wheel steady, reeling them in an inch at a time, teeth gritted, eyes up.

The sport punished him. Calves cramped, forearms burned, and the night before each meet he barely slept, replaying corners in the dark. Still, he was first at the gate at dawn, water bottle clenched like a lifeline.

Each checkered flag he grabbed shaved a slice off the sting of that first failure. Seven podiums out of the next nine races turned the whispers into cheers.

He didn’t chase trophies for the photos; he chased them because the early wipeout had taught him the worth of getting back up. The losses had carved out space for grit, and the wins simply filled it.

When the season closed, nobody remembered the kid who didn’t finish—they remembered the one who won seven out of ten. Kids in the crowd started wearing his number. And Lucas, still quiet beneath the visor, just smiled: fall hard, stand up harder.

The council shifted its attention to other corners of the budget after residents packed the chamber to defend libraries and arts programs. The idea of cutting culture spending died on the spot, drowned out by a chorus of “no.”

Raising parking fees was the next proposal to fall. Shoppers already skip the high street, merchants warned; pricier meters would only leave more empty storefronts. Letters and emails from residents echoed the fear, and the council backed off.

With those two levers gone, members went hunting for money elsewhere. They’ll ask the state for extra help, trim energy use in public buildings, squeeze more efficiency from every department, and chase down unpaid taxes. Supplier contracts are under fresh scrutiny, and talks with local firms about joint projects that could pump new life into the economy are under way.

Leaders admit none of this will be fun. Their promise: protect day-to-day services and keep daily life livable while they search for savings.

Neighbors exhaled—story hours, concerts, and free internet will stay, and a trip downtown won’t cost more at the curb. Still, everyone knows the relief could be short-lived; a yawning budget gap isn’t going away and tougher choices wait just around the corner.

Scottish independence isn’t a brand-new cause, but it has gathered real momentum in the past ten years. The Scottish National Party has put independence at the heart of its agenda, pushing the 2014 referendum that saw 45 % vote Yes and 55 % vote No. Walk down any high street and you’ll still hear “Scotland should be independent” from voters who reel off economic, cultural and political reasons for sticking with that view.

Supporters often start with the democratic deficit: Scotland elects 59 of the 650 MPs at Westminster, so laws that shape Scottish life are regularly passed by politicians the electorate never backed. The clearest example, they say, is Brexit—Scotland voted 62 % to stay in the EU, but was pulled out by England’s larger share of the vote.

Economically, backers point to North Sea oil, arguing the tax revenues could give a newly independent Scotland a generous starter fund. Add in a world-class renewable-energy sector, prime fishing grounds and a steady flow of tourists, and many picture a nimble, Nordic-style economy built on green power and social cohesion.

Culturally, Scotland keeps its own legal system, languages and traditions; independence campaigners feel these differences are flattened inside the Union.

Still, tearing up a 300-year-old treaty carries hazards: what currency would people use? Would there be a hard border with England? How long would EU re-entry talks take, and on what terms?

So the country remains split down the middle. Some say the question must be put again, soon; others insist the 2014 result should stand and warn against more division when the wider world already feels brittle.

Brian never pretended he was okay with the rot that had taken hold of the government—he’d run on a promise to drag it into the light. The ballots were barely counted before he reminded everyone that winning an election was nothing compared to the fight ahead: finding the billions that had vanished under earlier regimes and convincing a cynical public that honesty still had a seat at the table.

His first move was to create an anti-corruption unit that answered to no ministry, no party boss, no one but the truth. He stocked it with bloodhound auditors, prosecutors who’d already stared down death threats, and detectives whose idea of a good time was following a paper trail until it smoked. Their brief was simple: name the damage, count the cost, and follow the money wherever it led.

It didn’t take long to see how steep the climb would be. Every file they opened revealed three more, each thicker than the last. Lobbyists who treated laws like rental agreements and conglomerates that had bankrolled administrations for decades pushed back hard. Hearings turned into televised slugfests, impeachment motions landed like clockwork, and late-night comedians had a running bet on how many scandals one presidency could survive.

Brian kept showing up at the office before sunrise, sleeves rolled, coffee gone cold while he read through seized ledgers and intercepted emails. Slowly the picture emerged: shell companies inside shell companies, signatures that belonged to ghosts, and wire transfers hopping from Zurich to the Caymans and back again. The team mapped it all on a wall-sized chart that looked like a spider on LSD.

By the end of the first year they had handcuffed cabinet secretaries, frozen beachfront mansions, and emptied safes full of jewelry that had never seen daylight. For the first time in decades, the usual suspects stopped sounding invincible. Yet each headline came with a price—anonymous letters, brake lines cut, and one afternoon a bullet that punched through the window of his convoy, close enough to pepper his jacket with glass. He kept the jacket; he also kept going.

When term limits finally tapped him on the shoulder, Brian’s accountants announced they had clawed back hundreds of millions—nowhere near the full haul, but enough to pave roads, rebuild schools, and let mothers in rural clinics find medicine on the shelves again. He walked out of the palace the same way he’d walked in: no motorcade, no speech, just a quiet wave to the guards and the knowledge that the job wasn’t finished, only handed forward.

The country he left behind was still bruised, still skeptical, but no longer quite so sure that corruption was the only game in town.

Robin Bevan, head teacher at a Southend school, has spoken up about his unease with reducing children to numbers. At a recent governors’ meeting he warned that slapping scores on behaviour or achievement can twist what we think we know about a pupil and, worse, what the pupil thinks about themselves.

Numbers, he told the room, flatten the richness of learning. A tidy “7” or “85 %” feels precise, but it hides the child who is coasting, the one grieving, the one who has just discovered poetry yet still can’t spell. “Education is too messy, too human, for a spreadsheet,” Bevan said. “A single figure can’t hold the weight of a child’s context: poverty, curiosity, anxiety, the day their dog died.”

He gave an example: a Year 9 pupil who scores 90 % in maths looks stellar on paper, yet the grade masks the fact she’s bored, unstretched and quietly giving up. “We congratulate ourselves on the digit and miss the child,” Bevan said. “That’s not accuracy; it’s blindness.”

Instead of more data drops, he wants teachers swapping stories about what they see in class, pupils reflecting on their own next steps, and celebration of breakthroughs—like the boy who finally asked a question after three silent years—that will never fit a rubric. “We need to stop asking ‘What did you get?’ and start asking ‘What did you learn about yourself today?’”

Shifting the culture won’t be easy; league-table habits run deep. But Bevan believes that if parents, policy-makers and teachers keep talking, they can trade the mirage of precision for something closer to truth: a picture of each learner that is painted, not measured, into life.

It had been a war of attrition, ninety minutes of lungs burning and hearts thumping. All afternoon Blair Turgott had quietly kept the team afloat, a calm head while everything else turned frantic. The opposition were nasty, snapping at heels and refusing to drop, yet Turgott never flinched; his refusal to buckle lifted the whole pitch.

Every passage of play felt like walking a tight-rope—one slack moment and it was over. The clock bled away, nerves rose, and you could taste the doubt in the stands. Then Turgott zoned the noise out and took over.

A one-touch blur—left, right, left—carved space where none existed. The ball zipped along the grass, defenders left leaning the wrong way, and Turgott arrived like a train, clipping it first time. The keeper sprawled, the ball kissed the inside of the post and nestled.

For a heartbeat the ground stood still, then erupted. Scarves twirled, strangers hugged, and the scoreboard blinked a brand-new story written in the ninety-third minute.

Cool head, hot feet—Turgott had shown both. One swing of his right boot turned him from schemer to saviour and reminded everyone why you never leave early. The roar that followed felt like it could lift the roof off Grange Lane.

When the whistle finally came, supporters poured onto the grass, phones flashing, songs spilling out. The late, impossible win felt like a cup final in May, not a league game drifting toward a draw.

And at the centre of it stood Blair Turgott, shirt stuck to his chest, smile as wide as the valley. Ask anyone who saw it: on that day, at that hour, only one man was writing the script, and his name echoed long into the evening sky.

After twenty-two years, John Terry is finally saying goodbye to Chelsea. The one-club defender, who joined as a boy and leaves a legend, told fans on Instagram he won’t sign a new deal.  
“It’s been an absolute pleasure,” he wrote. “I’ve captained the team I love, shared a dressing room with heroes, and collected memories that will stay with me forever.”

Numbers back up the romance: 717 games, 67 goals, five Premier Leagues, five FA Cups, three League Cups, plus the Champions League and Europa League. This season, though, injuries limited him to nine appearances, a reminder that even icons slow down.

Now 36, Terry’s next step is anyone’s guess. MLS, coaching, TV—his phone hasn’t stopped buzzing. Whatever he chooses, he signs off with gratitude: “Thank you, Chelsea fans. Your support has been everything.”

The club hasn’t revealed farewell plans yet, but few doubt Stamford Bridge will find a way to honour its captain, leader, legend.

Last season’s champs reminded everyone why they’re still the team to beat, peppering the keeper with nearly fifty shots and never letting the pace drop. It was attack after attack—quick, clever, and ruthless whenever a half-chance appeared.

The story of the night, though, was Clare Shine. She walked off with the match ball after a hat-trick that had the crowd on its feet. Her first was pure foresight: a glide past two defenders and a low rocket inside the far post. The second came from a keeper’s fumble that she punished in a heartbeat, stabbing home the loose ball. The hat-trick goal was the prettiest—one touch to settle, another to swivel away from the last defender, then a curling finish that kissed the underside of the bar.

Three goals, three different answers to the same question: how do you turn pressure into points? The headlines belonged to Shine, but every sprint and pass around her carried the same swagger that delivered last season’s treble. 

And they’re not done. Pre-season has been harder, the game plan sharper; Shine and company are already plotting the next trophy.

Online booking sites have changed the way we plan vacations, weekend breaks, and business trips. With a few clicks we can reserve flights, rooms, cars, and even skip-the-line museum tickets.

Research shows the big draw is round-the-clock convenience. Because the sites never close, travelers can compare prices at midnight or rebook a flight from the airport lounge without waiting on hold. Everything lives in one window, so there’s no need to open a dozen tabs.

The inventory helps, too. Global partnerships mean thousands of hotels, airlines, and rental brands appear side by side, letting shoppers weigh cost, timing, and perks in minutes instead of hours. For suppliers, that visibility can fill empty seats and beds; for consumers, it keeps prices honest—though hotels grumble about the steep commissions.

Still, the do-it-yourself model has drawbacks. There’s no agent to call when plans unravel, and changing a non-refundable fare can feel like wrestling a robot. A glitchy app or an unresponsive chatbot can turn a dream trip into a headache fast, so it pays to scan recent user reviews before handing over a credit card.

Bottom line: online booking engines have made travel planning faster, cheaper, and more transparent than ever, but a quick reputation check and a careful read of the fine print can save plenty of trouble later.

I nodded and kept going. “We each tame panic in our own way. Some crank the dial to full-throttle focus, scrubbing the kitchen at 3 a.m. or rewriting spreadsheets until the font bleeds. It’s not meltdown—it’s steering the wheel so the car stays on the road.”

While I talked control, my brain flicked through its own highlight reel: nights when deadlines stacked like Jenga, the last block wobbling, my heartbeat loud enough to drown the fridge hum. Panic always parked nearby, engine idling.

“But listen,” I said, “scared is just a radio station we all get. The trick is whether we let it blast, or sample the beat and remix it into forward motion.”

The room had gone still, the kind of quiet where you hear the HVAC sigh. I couldn’t tell if I was preaching or just thinking out loud, yet the words kept sliding out, smooth and necessary.

“Bottom line: fear doesn’t get fired. It gets promoted to the department that keeps you awake, creative, alive. Courage isn’t the absence of panic; it’s the conversation you have with it so it works for you instead of against you.”

A beat later, heads bobbed—small, thoughtful nods like ripples across a pond. My chest unclenched; someone else’s recognition felt like cool water on a burn.

A voice floated up: “Thanks—that really helps.”

I smiled, small and real. Saying the scary stuff out loud didn’t make me a target; it built a bridge. Turns out acceptance travels both ways, and panic loses its grip when it’s met by a roomful of nodding strangers who suddenly feel like teammates.

Back in 1973, researchers launched a study that’s still running today: every ten years they check in on the same group of kids—who now have kids of their own. What began as a snapshot of childhood has turned into a moving picture of growing up, showing how early life echoes decades later.

Teams don’t just measure height and weight; they sit down with participants to talk moods, friendships, report cards, and later, jobs and paychecks. When home computers, then smartphones, showed up, the scientists added questions about screen time, online bullying, and anxious nights.

Because the families come from every walk of life, the data can tease out how money, neighborhoods, and schools shape adulthood. The big picture keeps showing the same story: kids who grow up surrounded by books and encouraging adults tend to climb higher in school, and those who run around at recess are still running at forty-five.

The volunteers are now middle-aged, so the study is shifting toward gray hair, sore knees, and how soon people can afford to retire. Fresh crews of babies join every decade to keep the lens wide.

In short, this living time machine keeps teaching us how today’s small choices become tomorrow’s big patterns—and policymakers keep listening.

London’s National Portrait Gallery needs to raise £100,000 to keep a rare treasure from slipping into private hands. The painting shows Ayuba Suleiman Diallo—better known as Job ben Solomon—a learned Muslim prince seized by slave traders in 1730 and shipped to America. Even in bondage he kept his faith, taught Arabic to fellow captives, and won admiration for his intellect and character. William Hoare captured that quiet dignity in 1733 while Diallo was in England; the canvas is now the earliest British portrait to portray a black sitter as an individual, not a stereotype.

Every pound pledged keeps the picture on public walls where it belongs. The gallery has already gathered most of the money, but still needs £100,000; gifts from individuals, companies, and trusts will close the gap. Keeping Diallo’s gaze in the nation’s collection lets tomorrow’s visitors of every background see a fuller, fairer story of Britain.

Crossing the border is only the first hurdle. Once in the Dominican Republic, Haitian migrants routinely run into abuse, prejudice, and a system that treats them as disposable. The DR may look prosperous next to Haiti, but pockets of deep poverty and scarce jobs still haunt both nations.

The two neighbors share an island and a tangled past of wars, race politics, and boom-and-bust cycles. A thin, lightly guarded line divides them, and every day thousands of Haitians step across it, papers or no papers, chasing the promise of steady wages.

Dominican plantations, building sites, and kitchens hunger for cheap, unskilled labor—work most citizens won’t touch. Haitians fill the gap, but the pay is a pittance, the shifts are brutal, and a raid or deportation can come at any moment. That fear keeps people quiet when bosses withhold wages or demand longer hours.

Worse, hostility follows them home. Darker skin and a Haitian surname are often enough for harassment. Since 2010 the government has rewritten its citizenship rules, and people who were born and raised here suddenly find they don’t belong anywhere. A 2013 Constitutional Court ruling stripped nationality from anyone whose parents couldn’t prove legal status back to 1929, leaving tens of thousands stateless. The United Nations condemned the decision as arbitrary and discriminatory, but the court stood firm, souring relations between Port-au-Prince and Santo Domingo.

Aid groups keep pushing for a softer policy—emergency documents, birth-registry drives, legal-aid clinics—yet the backlash is fierce. Officials insist the country is already overcrowded and can’t carry Haiti’s poor.

Still, the boats and buses roll north. For most migrants, even a precarious job in the DR beats the hunger and violence they left behind. Their journey is a gamble for dignity, mirrored in every borderland on the planet.

The site was wrapped in a hush so thick it felt hard to breathe. Hard-hatted crews in neon vests picked through the broken concrete one careful handful at a time, every scrape of metal on stone echoing like a warning. No one needed reminding what was at stake: three friends were still buried somewhere beneath their boots, and the waiting families were living every second of it.

Everything had stopped the moment the boiler house came down. Investigators moved in first, sealing the scene, triple-checking that the next shift wouldn’t be digging out their own. For the loved ones pacing the car-park, the hours crawled; for the crews used to dust and noise, the stillness was its own kind of collapse.

Hope and dread took turns in every chest. Jokes died mid-sentence, replaced by quiet nods and the soft clink of harnesses. Every man there had sworn the same silent oath: we bring our own home, no matter what.

Handlers worked the search dogs in slow, overlapping grids, letting the animals’ noses do what machines still can’t. Above them, yesterday’s drone video ran on loop inside the command trailer—frame by frame, looking for any gap, any shadow that might be a pocket where life could still cling.

Running the show was the rescue chief, thirty years of disasters tucked into the creases around his eyes. He moved from zone to zone without hurry, speaking little, measuring the weight of every decision against the three faces taped to the site-office wall. The lines around his mouth said what his voice wouldn’t: we will find them, and it will hurt.

By sunset the floodlights took over from the failing sun. No one cheered, no one quit; they simply stepped back, helmets in hand, forming a loose circle on the cracked asphalt. No speeches, just the low hum of generators and the unspoken vow that tomorrow they’d be back before first light, ready to keep the promise made to mothers, wives, and kids who hadn’t slept in two nights.

Scarthin Books, the much-loved Cromford landmark, needs a bit of muscle to keep carrying its ever-growing family of volumes. With more than 100,000 books spread over several floors, the old Derbyshire building is starting to feel the strain, so a careful upgrade is underway.

Four tailor-made steel columns, designed to share the load without shouting for attention, will soon slip into the quiet corners of the shop. Placed where footsteps already flow, they’ll keep the shelves upright and the browsing calm, while blending with the timeworn charm of the place.

Stonewall and Hampstead, a local practice that knows its way around heritage timbers, is sketching the details. They’re promising columns that look like they always belonged—more bookmark than eyesore—while giving the building the backbone it needs for another century of stories.

Alongside the steel, the team will freshen up the ventilation and swap tired wooden supports for sturdier sisters. Work will roll out in stages, one floor at a time, so the tills can stay open and the coffee machine keeps puffing. Sections may shuffle about for a week or two, but no genre will vanish entirely.

When the dust settles, Scarthin Books should stand straighter, breathe easier and still feel like the cosy warren readers have always wandered. The shelves will be safer, the future roomier, and the next chapter ready for whoever turns the page.

Carl James isn’t just another guy in a galaxy far, far away—he’s the Star Wars superfan every collector whispers about at toy fairs. Ask around and you’ll hear how Carl can sniff out a diamond-in-the-rough Jawa or a double-telescoping lightsaber the way a Jedi senses a disturbance in the Force.

His latest coup? A scruffy-looking Boba Fett he grabbed for pocket change at a neighborhood garage sale just fetched £15,000, landing him on breakfast TV and in every collector’s group chat. Carl still shakes his head at the memory. “I only stopped for the donuts,” he jokes.

Now he’s ready to let go of fifteen more treasures he’s quietly hoarded since childhood: the original 32-inch Millennium Falcon studio model, Vader’s helmet signed by Dave Prowse, and carded figures of Luke, Leia and Yoda so pristine they look like they just left the toy aisle in 1978.

Carl’s confident the pieces will find good homes—Star Wars fans have never been shy about opening their wallets—but he admits the emotional price is steeper. “Every dent, every scuff is a memory,” he says. “Still, I’d rather see them flying across someone else’s display case than sitting in mine collecting dust.”

Word of the auction has already ignited Reddit threads from California to Christchurch. Dealers, historians and nostalgic thirty-somethings are marking calendars, because when Carl drops his collection, the aftermarket will feel the tremor. Decades after the first film hit theaters, the Force—at least in collectible form—remains strong with this one.

It happened in the blink of an eye: a teenage boy no one is naming allegedly lunged at Gwen Louden in the courthouse foyer last January.  

People waiting for their own cases still flinch when they talk about it. Because the law shields both minors and assault victims, every witness asked to stay anonymous. “No warning, no argument—he just went at her,” one said quietly.  

Gwen, a woman most locals know from charity drives, had simply stopped in to sort out a small civil matter. Friends say she still has no idea why she was singled out.  

Detective Francis Barnes, lead on the investigation, admits they’re stumped. “Right now it looks random, but we’re chasing every possible reason,” he told reporters.  

Court security officers swarmed in seconds, pinned the teen, and later added a contempt citation on top of the assault charge.  

Gwen’s daughter, Michelle, fought back tears. “Mum’s sixty-eight. Who does this to a grandmother?” She paused, then thanked the guards: “Without them, it could have been so much worse.”  

Gwen is now in a nearby hospital, listed in stable condition. Doctors say rest—and counselling—will take time. Her family has asked for space to breathe.  

The boy’s case moves to juvenile court; if the assault and contempt charges stick, he’ll be sentenced within that system.  

The episode has reopened a broader debate about how safe public areas of the courthouse really are. Administrators have already pledged a full review of foyer security and promised changes so no one else has to walk through the doors fearing what happened to Gwen Louden.

An inquest heard that 37-year-old Mark Staley from West Bridgeford struck Sally Shalloe while pulling out to overtake on the busy road.

Sally, a mum who gave countless hours to local causes, lived for fresh air and exercise; her bike was part of her everyday life. Her sudden death stunned Attenborough, the village she called home.

Witnesses said the crash flung her from the bicycle. Passers-by fought to save her and paramedics arrived within minutes, yet the injuries proved fatal.

Tom, her husband of twenty-five years, and their grown-up sons Ben and Leo are struggling to take in the loss.  
“Sally was the centre of us,” Tom said. “It helps a little to know she was outside, doing what she loved, not sick or frightened.”

Investigators found Staley was within the speed limit, but judged his overtaking move “rash and dangerous”; he now faces a charge of causing death by dangerous driving. The trial opens next week at Nottingham Crown Court.

The village has wrapped its arms around the family. Hundreds packed the local church for Sally’s memorial, and plans are under way to name a new cycle path after her.

Beyond her family, she was the quiet force behind the wildlife-trust work parties and litter-picks that kept the nature reserves thriving. Her absence leaves a hole that volunteers say will be hard to fill.

The tragedy has also restarted debate about keeping cyclists safe, with neighbours petitioning for protected lanes and tighter rules on overtaking, determined that another family should not face the same heartbreak.

Everyone had been waiting for this night, and Hollywood showed up in force. A-list actors, award-winning directors, and power-broker producers flew in from every coast, stepping onto the crimson carpet while flashbulbs popped like popcorn. Reporters shouted questions; publicists steered talent from one velvet rope to the next. Glamour felt like a second skin here.

Outside the barricades, the sidewalk pulsed. Fans packed shoulder-to-shoulder, waving homemade signs and worn-out DVDs, voices cracking as they screamed first names that somehow felt like personal friends. The echo off the glass towers turned cheers into a single, roaring wave that rose and fell with each new limousine.

Inside the landmark theater, the air was thick with perfume and anticipation. Velvet seats disappeared under tuxedos and silk as ushers pointed the way; whispers rippled through the rows like wind across wheat. Word spread that the leads might say a few words before the curtain rose, and the rumor alone kept necks craned toward the stage.

The cast worked the room like seasoned politicians—quick jokes for the press, soft eyes for the kids pressed against the barricades, Sharpies gliding over glossy headshots. Between handshakes they stole glances at the ceiling, as if reminding themselves this moment was real, that years of shooting now came down to one heartbeat before the screen lit up.

Champagne flutes never seemed to empty. Plates of miniature crab cakes appeared and vanished. Conversations jumped from weekend grosses to vacation homes, all dressed up in sequins, velvet, and the kind of jewelry that needs its own security detail. Flamboyance wasn’t just accepted; it was the evening’s dress code.

Then the city seemed to inhale and hold it. The last stragglers hurried past the deserted carpet; traffic lights blinked to no one. Inside, the lobby lights dimmed twice—the universal cue to find your seat. The hum of conversation dropped to a hush punctuated only by the rustle of settling fabric. Trailers vanished, the curtain widened, and the first frame flickered to life. Two hours of hope, money, and sleepless nights unspooled in the dark, and for everyone in that room, nothing else existed.

Gloucester stretched their lead straight after the break with a penalty, but Exeter weren’t rattled for long; Jack Nowell dived over in the corner to haul them back into it. Wave after wave of Chiefs attacks followed, yet Gloucester’s defence refused to bend.

Twenty minutes from time Billy Twelvetrees nudged the hosts three points further ahead, and when Nic White darted under the sticks it looked as though Exeter might finally turn the screw. Instead, Twelvetrees kept the scoreboard ticking and, at 25-15, Sam Simmonds’ late try gave the Chiefs a sniff—until Willie Heinz smashed that hope with a breakaway score of his own.

There would be no grandstand finish; the final whistle confirmed a 30-20 win for Gloucester. Afterwards, director of rugby Johan Ackermann praised his side’s grit and saluted Exeter’s effort, acknowledging that the result lifts Gloucester up the table and sets up a tasty clash with Saracens next weekend. For Exeter, the defeat stings: they travel to Harlequins knowing standards must rise if they’re to stay among the league’s front-runners.

The company’s pension hole has swollen so large that it’s now a dead weight on the balance sheet. Years of topping up the fund couldn’t keep pace with lousy markets and rock-bottom rates, and the shortfall keeps widening.

Handing the whole obligation over to the Pension Protection Fund—or to an insurer that eats pension risk for breakfast—would lift the ball and chain and let management get back to running the business. The cash freed up could be ploughed into growth instead of plugging an ever-deeper hole.

But it’s not a simple sale; watchdogs have to pick the deal apart. The PPF exists to catch workers when employers go bust, so it will check that the company still owns enough assets to back every promise and that scheme members won’t be left worse off.

Unsurprisingly, employees and pensioners are jittery. Management has been holding town-halls and sending updates stressing that, whatever happens, their accrued rights stay protected under the rules. Union reps are parked at the table too, demanding full transparency and a hard look at any knock-on effects for staff and retirees.

Now the decision sits with the regulators, who must weigh the firm’s survival against member security. Staff, retirees and the market are all waiting for the verdict that will decide the company’s next chapter.

Otto Warmbier, a University of Virginia student, was grabbed by North Korean authorities while on a group tour in January 2016 and, a few weeks later, paraded before cameras as a confessed enemy of the state. A court handed him fifteen years in a labor camp.

On Tuesday his parents shared the news no one wanted to hear: their son had died, just six days after arriving home in a coma following seventeen months in custody. A U.S. coroner is now trying to piece together exactly what killed him.

President Trump responded with rare, raw anger. “Otto’s fate deepens my Administration’s determination to keep innocent people from suffering at the hands of regimes that have no regard for law or human decency,” he said, promising to stop anything similar from happening again.

Pyongyang still claims Warmbier slipped into a coma after contracting botulism and taking a sleeping pill, but American doctors who examined him say there’s no sign of that; they believe he may have suffered a catastrophic head injury.

The tragedy lands on already-frayed U.S.–North Korea ties, and Capitol Hill is already talking about tougher sanctions in Warmbier’s name.

Richard Howitt, who has represented the East of England in the European Parliament since 1994, is stepping down to become CEO of the International Integrated Reporting Council. The IIRC brings together regulators, investors, companies, standard-setters, accountants and NGOs to help business connect more meaningfully with society and the wider economy.

Howitt’s brief is to speed up worldwide uptake of integrated reporting—an approach that blends financial, environmental, social and governance data so stakeholders get a fuller picture of how a company really performs. It’s a natural fit for an MEP who has spent decades championing sustainability and corporate responsibility.

“I see integrated reporting as the future of corporate disclosure,” Howitt said. “I’m honoured to lead the IIRC’s drive for global adoption of these frameworks. When companies report in a more rounded way, they become more accountable and transparent, and that feeds into a healthier global economy.”

He will stay on in Strasbourg until he formally takes up the post later this year.

IIRC chair Mervyn King welcomed the appointment: “Richard’s track-record and passion for responsible business mirror our own ambitions. We’re convinced he’ll push corporate transparency and accountability to new levels.”

Howitt has been part of the IIRC family since its launch in 2010 and is the European Parliament’s rapporteur on corporate social responsibility—experience that leaves him well-prepared for the job.

His move highlights the gathering momentum behind the idea that companies should measure and disclose their impact on people, planet and profit alike, a shift expected to strengthen accountability and long-term value for all stakeholders.

David Waddington was the kind of Conservative who could silence a room with a raised eyebrow and a perfectly timed barb. Born in Burnley on 2 August 1929, he trained as a barrister before swapping the courtroom for the Commons, where his dry Lancastrian humour and unflappable manner quickly marked him out.

He first won a seat in 1968, becoming MP for Nelson and Colne, and later for Ribble Valley from 1983 until 1990. Along the way he collected the jobs no one else wanted—Chief Whip, Home Office minister—serving Margaret Thatcher with the same brisk efficiency he had once reserved for cross-examinations.

Then came the spring of 1990. As Home Secretary he inherited two crises that would land on every front page: the Strangeways riot and the poll-tax protests. The Manchester prison revolt dragged on for twenty-five days, the longest in British history, sparked by overcrowding and squalid conditions. When the smoke cleared, two men were dead and the Victorian wings were in ruins. Waddington authorised the operation that retook the jail, and the subsequent Woolf inquiry overhauled the entire prison system.

Weeks later, central London echoed to running battles between police and demonstrators furious at the poll tax. Windows shattered, charges and counter-charges swept through Trafalgar Square, and overnight the tax—and Thatcher—became mortally wounded. Critics accused Waddington of sending in too many boots; allies said he had stopped the capital from tipping into anarchy.

By November Thatcher was gone. John Major moved Waddington upstairs to lead the House of Lords, a post he held until 1992, when he stepped away as Baron Waddington of Read. The controversies never quite faded, yet colleagues still speak of a man who would not bend when the wind blew hardest, and whose steadiness—right or wrong—helped steady Britain’s course at a turbulent hour.

The report makes it clear that, although plenty of policies and initiatives claim to help older people who need care, the reality is patchy: only two-thirds of those who qualify actually receive meaningful support. That leaves well over a million older Britons scrambling for help, leaning on relatives or simply going without. Of the 1.5 million over-65s whose care needs go unmet, roughly 700,000 get no assistance whatsoever.

Day-to-day, this gap translates into real pain: frailty, anxiety, falls that could have been prevented, and families running on empty. Left unchecked, the lack of early help funnels seniors toward hospitals and crisis services, piling pressure on an already stretched NHS.

Age UK’s review warns that, with the over-65 cohort growing faster than any other age group, the government has to treat the crisis as urgent. The charity wants ministers to sit down with older people and their carers to design a system that actually works, not just on paper but in kitchens and living rooms across the country. Quick fixes are needed now—respite for exhausted relatives, clear information about entitlements, and emergency support for those who have fallen through the cracks.

Longer term, the review calls for a properly funded social-care settlement, easy-to-navigate advice services, and recognition of unpaid carers. Without sustained investment, the report concludes, today’s shortfalls could snowball into a full-blown emergency that engulfs health and social care within the decade.

Ever since little Gomez hit the headlines, the whole country has been holding its breath. The tiny marmoset—lone survivor of the troop that lived in a nearby private zoo before it went bust last year—has somehow wriggled his way into thousands of hearts.

When the gates slammed shut, the owners couldn’t place every creature; most were scooped up by a local rescue, but the marmoset family slipped through the cracks. One by one they vanished, until only Gomez was left. Someone—no one knows who—left him on the vet clinic steps, trembling, dehydrated, and too scared to move.

Staff called police and animal control the instant they spotted the shoebox bundle. Gomez was so thin his ribs counted themselves, and he flinched at every sound. Authorities have since opened a full investigation, and tip money—covered by donations from horrified neighbors and strangers across the country—keeps climbing for leads that end in a conviction.

For now, Gomez lives in the same hospital where he was dumped. The team whispers when they enter the room; even the clatter of food bowls sends him scrambling. Still, he’s eating, drinking, and—on good days—curling his tail round a fluffy toy monkey that stands in for the family he lost.

Behind the scenes, keepers are planning slow-motion play-dates with other marmosets, but only when he’s ready. Progress is measured in grams gained and seconds of eye contact held, yet every tiny step makes the evening news and pulls fresh hearts into the cause.

Gomez’s ordeal has turned spotlights on weak zoo oversight and patchy rehoming laws. Petitions are flooding lawmakers’ desks, and conservation groups are riding the wave of marmoset-mania, funneling new donations into protecting wild troops before they need rescuing at all.

What began as one fragile life tossed aside is fast becoming a national push for kinder rules and fuller protection—proof that even the smallest monkey can shake a very big tree.

Nobody was injured, but the empty, grade-listed pub is now a blackened shell and experts still don’t know what sparked the blaze.

“We got the first 999 call just after nine last night,” said Roger Jenkins of South Wales Fire and Rescue. “Neighbors reported smoke and flames punching through the roof.”

Within an hour the fire had taken hold, drawing crews from half the county. At the height of the operation thirty firefighters, six pumps, an aerial platform and a water bowser were battling to stop the flames leaping to nearby homes.

“The roof and first floor were already well alight when we arrived,” Jenkins said. “Conditions were brutal, but the crews stopped it spreading beyond the pub.”

Families on the adjoining streets were evacuated as a precaution; many spent the night in the village hall, looked after by Red Cross volunteers. They were allowed back just after sunrise.

By dawn the fire was out, though crews stayed on scene to hose down smouldering beams and keep the public clear.

“We did everything we could to save the fabric, but the damage is extensive,” Jenkins admitted. “The roof’s gone and the upper floor has collapsed—any restoration will be a major project.”

Police tape now flutters around the former White Hart, an eighteenth-century coaching inn that has stood empty for years. Once investigators can get inside they’ll hunt for a cause; arson hasn’t been ruled out.

“We won’t guess,” Jenkins said. “This place matters to people. We’ll give them answers as soon as we safely can.”

Locals, who had been raising funds to reopen the pub, are already talking about rebuilding. “It’s part of our story,” one resident said. “We’ll bring it back, brick by brick.”

Nelson Packaging has confirmed it is laying off staff, saying the move is unavoidable after months of sliding sales. The Lancashire plant, best known for its bespoke packaging, has been hit hard by the global slowdown.

Posts have gone across the shop floor and the office, trimming the workforce to a level that will inevitably slow output. Union reps warn the cuts will send fresh shocks through a local economy already reeling from the pandemic.

HR says its sole focus now is helping people leave with dignity: one-to-one career coaching, upskilling courses and counselling sessions are being rolled out for everyone affected.

The town’s MP has urged Whitehall to step in. “This many jobs lost at once is devastating,” she said. “We need emergency support for the workers and real investment to attract new employers.”

The company admits the path back will be steep: battered demand, rising costs and the virus’s lingering drag all lie ahead. Executives said the decision “kept them awake at night” and pledged to stand by every colleague through the upheaval.

Whether staff who remain will still feel secure enough to give their best is the unanswered question hanging over the factory’s future.

The defeat stung, but it also jolted the Scots awake. Up to then they’d flickered rather than blazed—flashes of slick passing quickly smothered by sloppy decisions. In the dressing-room the veteran coach gathered his staff and scribbled two words on the whiteboard: “fix it.”

At the next meeting he kept it short. “We’re not a bunch of soloists,” he told them. “We lose the ball because we chase glory, and we miss chances because no one gambles on the second ball.” From now on every session would finish with a score-at-all-costs drill; every player would track back as if his boots were on fire. “Treat the next game like a cup final,” he said, “because it basically is.”

Heads were low, yet no one panicked. They still had thirteen outfielders who could spray a forty-metre pass and a keeper who bailed them out weekly. What they needed was honesty and repetition—nothing mystical, just hard graft. The captain set the tone, arriving early, staying late, demanding one more set, one more sprint, until the floodlights clicked off.

Within a fortnight the same group looked unrecognisable. They pinged triangles around press-resistant midfielders, the back line stepped up in perfect sync, and the striker timed his diagonal run to meet the clipped cross. Three wins on the spin turned whispers of an early flight home into talk of last-sixteen hotels.

Climbing the table felt surreal, but the lesson was simple: an opening stumble doesn’t write the script; the pages that follow do. Start ugly, finish proud—if you’re willing to run through walls, the story can still end with silver glinting under the summer sun.

Over the same stretch, the number of patients who had to be shipped out to another hospital climbed from 60 in 2011-12 to 75 in 2014-15. At the same time, readmissions to the ICU during the same stay inched down from 4.5 % to 4.3 %.

Deaths on the unit eased off a little, sliding from 15 % to 14.5 %, but the 30-day toll after discharge crept up from 18.2 % to 18.5 %.  

Patients were getting out faster too: the average stay shrank from 2.8 days to 2.5, probably thanks to slicker treatments or smoother step-down care. The gender split stayed almost flat, with women making up 42.5–43.3 % of admissions.

Taken together, the numbers paint a picture of busier ICUs, quicker turnovers and stubborn post-discharge risks. The workload isn’t letting up, and if the gains are to stick, hospitals will need more than a quick fix—they’ll need a plan.

They kicked off looking sluggish—passes rolling to nobody, sitters skied, the crowd groaning louder with every misfire. You could feel the players shrink, as if the shirt had suddenly grown two sizes too heavy.

Then, out of nowhere, Harry Maguire thundered in a header from a corner. The stadium blinked, then roared; the big defender had jump-started United’s pulse. Minutes later Daniel James tore down the wing, left two defenders on the grass and slid the ball home. Two-nil, breathing space at last.

Late drama followed: a soft penalty, the away end hushed, hearts in mouths. David de Gea guessed right, clawed it away, and the travelling fans finally exhaled.

It was messy, nothing like the swagger of old, but three points on the road feel like gold when confidence has been running on fumes. Ole called it “ugly but necessary,” and supporters flew home daring to believe the corner might—just might—have been turned.

Barry Pring, a 47-year-old IT consultant from Devon, had flown to Kiev to see the woman he’d married after meeting her on an international dating site. Ganna Ziuzina, barely in her twenties, still lived in Ukraine while Barry worked in Britain. On the night of their first anniversary the couple went out to celebrate; after dinner Barry, drunk and disoriented, wandered into the road to flag a taxi and was mown down.

What looked like a routine hit-and-run quickly turned into front-page news on both sides of Europe. Local police logged it as an accident, but Barry’s relatives refused to accept the verdict. A coroner’s inquest opened in 2011, stalled, and then quietly went cold.

Six years later the story flipped. A High Court judge quashed the accidental-death ruling and recorded an unlawful killing. Attention swung to Ganna—now calling herself Julianne Moore—who had never been treated as a suspect. The court was told she may have deliberately steered her husband into the path of the car so she could claim his £1.5 million estate. She denied everything, insisting she loved Barry and was shattered by his death.

The inquiry that followed became a tug-of-war: Barry’s family shouting murder, Ganna producing love-struck emails, the other side replying with transcripts of furious rows. In late 2019 she agreed to answer questions from British detectives, but only as a witness. Interviews and forensic reviews dragged deep into 2021, yet no charges were brought.

Today the file is still open. Barry’s relatives campaign for justice; Ganna claims she is being hounded by vengeful in-laws. Somewhere between Devon and Kiev the truth lies buried, leaving two countries and one broken family no closer to knowing who, if anyone, pushed Barry Pring under that speeding car.

Turnbull still believes Australia should ditch the monarchy, but insists the push has to come from the street, not Parliament. “It only sticks if it bubbles up from the suburbs and the schools, not if it’s handed down by politicians,” the former PM said.  

He remembers the bruising ’99 referendum—back then he ran Australians for Constitutional Monarchy—only too well. “One inglorious loss is enough for a lifetime; I’m not keen on a sequel.”

His remarks threw the republic back onto kitchen tables and talkback radio, where it has drifted for thirty years. Polls keep saying “yeah, maybe,” yet that yes rarely rings loud enough to make Canberra move.  

“If you want it,” Turnbull told voters, “you’ll have to shout in unison—loud enough that no one can pretend they didn’t hear.” The comment felt less like observation, more like a starter’s gun.

Still, he admits the finish line may sit beyond his horizon. “The planets would all have to line up,” he shrugged, “but I’ll keep waving the flag until they do.”

Success, he added, means a marathon, not a sprint: “Until ordinary Australians stand up and stay standing, a referendum is just an expensive opinion poll.” With that, the old republican handed the baton back to the people, hoping this time they’d run with it.

Arthur Cory, the eldest son of the late Lord Penllyn, grew up in the long shadow of Penllyn Castle, the family’s weather-beaten fortress outside Cowbridge. The place has towered over Welsh fields for centuries, and so has the Cory name. Tucked away in a dim cupboard Arthur found a relic he’d almost forgotten: an old flag, creased and mended so many times it looked like a patchwork of stories.

Green and white, with a red dragon breathing fire, it was more than the national symbol—it was his father’s travelling companion from younger, rebellious days. Lord Penllyn had once marched every Welsh parade with that dragon snapping above his head, but mortgages, meetings, and finally illness folded the flag away with the rest of his youth.

When Arthur shook the dust from the linen, the colours were still defiantly bright. As he spread it across the study floor, the room filled with the faint smell of bonfire smoke and rugby pitches, of poems read aloud in cramped student rooms. Aunt Mabel, whisky in hand, told him how his father used the flag as a curtain, a tablecloth, even a blanket during long nights of protest. Friends from those years wrote letters describing a lanky, red-cheeked Penllyn waving the dragon like a battle standard, promising anyone who listened that Wales would never be just a footnote in Britain’s story.

Each anecdote stitched Arthur closer to a man he had only known in suits and silences. The dragon, he realised, wasn’t just mythic—it was his father’s portrait: stubborn, passionate, impossible to ignore.

Arthur pressed the flag, hemmed the frayed edge, and hung it where the morning sun strikes the castle’s entrance hall. He tells his children the stories as they climb the broad staircase, letting the dragon’s shadow ripple across their faces, carrying the old fire forward.

Doctors everywhere say the same thing: if we don’t reach people soon enough, small problems snowball into emergencies. It happens in mental-health clinics, in cancer wards, in every corridor of medicine.

Catch an illness early and the odds flip in the patient’s favor. But too many people still wait—because the next appointment is months away, the clinic is miles off, or the insurance won’t stretch. While they wait, depression deepens, tumors grow, arteries clog. What could have been solved with a few sessions of therapy or a quick excision becomes a fight for life.

The suicide statistics alone make the case: thousands every day who might have been saved by a timely conversation. The same goes for cancers that are curable in stage one and incurable in stage four; the difference is a screening that never happened.

Phones that spot irregular heartbeats, scans that find a speck-sized tumor, watches that notice you haven’t slept in days—tech is doing its part. Yet the system underneath creaks: not enough nurses, not enough money, and whole postal codes without a single clinic. Rural towns and low-income neighborhoods feel the gaps first.

When we miss the window, the price isn’t paid only by the patient. Ambulances, ICUs, chemo suites, and mortuaries all fill up, and the economy quietly bleeds billions that prevention would have spared.

Governments have to stop treating health policy like a ambulance service and start running it like a fence at the cliff’s edge. That means teaching people what to look for, paying doctors to look before symptoms scream, and building clinics where they’re actually needed.

If we screen, educate, staff, and open the doors wider, crises shrink. A ten-minute chat or a routine scan can turn a future tragedy into a manageable detour—and leave the system strong enough to care for the next person in line.

Uncovered in 2005, the wooden fish weir has been quietly telling the story of the people who once lived along the edge of Southampton Water. Hundreds of sharpened stakes, driven into the sand, formed a V-shaped fence that fish blundered into at low tide; the catch could simply be scooped up.  

Archaeologists rarely get this lucky. Sea-level sites normally rot, shift or wash away, so finding a timber trap that has sat in salt water for more than twelve centuries feels like stumbling on an intact Viking ship in a swimming pool. The stakes, tool-marks and a few lost iron knives point to Anglo-Saxon hands around 700 AD, while the bones wedged between the posts read like a medieval menu: salmon, sea trout and the occasional eel – fast food for folk who lived within sight of the tide.

Southampton has taken the weir to heart. Once the recording and conservation work is finished, the council wants to fold the site into a small archaeological park so walkers can stand where the builders stood and picture the traps filling at dusk. Tour guides already weave the weir into harbour walks, and a handful of local fishing clubs have started running “heritage casts” that pair modern rods with stories of Saxon ingenuity.

Word has travelled: dendrochronologists, geo-archaeologists, marine biologists and even culinary historians have asked for samples, each hoping the river-stained wood or the ancient fish DNA will add another piece to the puzzle of how early English communities coaxed dinner from the sea. What began as a routine pre-development survey has become a meeting place for disciplines and centuries, a fragile line of stakes that still ties the city to its past.

According to the RAC – one of Britain’s most respected motoring bodies – drivers are being hit by a perfect storm. Crude oil has been creeping steadily upward, dragging petrol, diesel and jet-fuel prices with it. At the same time, the weaker Pound that followed the Brexit vote makes every imported litre more expensive, so the cost at the pump climbs even faster. In short, world markets and home-grown politics are both squeezing the UK motorist.

The RAC doesn’t see the pressure easing any time soon. If oil keeps rising and Brexit uncertainty lingers, household and business budgets will tighten still further, on top of the financial pain already caused by Covid-19.

The club is calling on the government to soften the blow, perhaps by trimming fuel duty or the VAT share of each litre. For their part, drivers can help themselves by choosing more economical cars or leaving the car at home whenever there’s a practical alternative.

Iffley Academy, which teaches 8- to 18-year-olds with special needs, is changing its name after worried parents pointed out that people were mistaking it for the extremist group ISIS. The final straw came when the militants launched an online channel called “Isis Academy.”

Head teacher Kay Willett says the link is pure coincidence, but protecting pupils comes first. “Our job is to keep children and staff safe. Sharing a name with a terrorist organisation creates risk we can’t ignore,” she explained.

Because the school sits on Iffley Turn in Oxford, slipping the street name into the title felt obvious. After talking it through with families, students and neighbours, the switch to “Iffley Academy” won near-unanimous backing.

Councillor John Howson praised the decision: “No one should have to rename a school for something so unconnected, yet their focus on student welfare is spot-on.”

Willett promises nothing else will change. “Same teachers, same values, same determination to help every child thrive,” she said. Letters, signs and websites are already being updated, and parents say they can already feel the relief.

Sir Nicholas Winton was the quiet hero who, in 1938, walked away from a skiing holiday in Switzerland after a friend begged him to visit Prague instead. A London stockbroker by trade, he arrived to find Nazi Germany already swallowing the Sudetenland and Jewish families frantic to get their children out.

Winton set up an office in a borrowed room and, between cups of terrible coffee, began filling forms, bribing officials, and sweet-talking British customs officers. One by one he pieced together trains, foster homes, and entry permits for 669 boys and girls who left Prague on eight kindertransports before war closed the borders. When paperwork stalled, he quietly invented it; when money ran short, he dipped into his own pocket.

Back home he carried on lobbying Parliament, lining up quarantine facilities, and meeting trains at Liverpool Street long after the Blitz made every journey a gamble. Then the war swallowed Europe and, with it, the story of what he had done. For half a century Winton never mentioned the scrapbook in the attic; only in 1988 did his wife open the dusty album of photographs, lists, and thank-you notes and ask, “Whose children are these?”

The wider Kindertransport he helped inspire eventually saved around 10,000 young lives, yet Winton always shrugged off the spotlight. The man who came to be called “the British Schindler” simply said he only did what any decent person would have done—then went back to his garden.

The Dons hadn’t won at home in months and you could feel it—every tackle, every cheer carried the weight of that drought. Inside a quarter-hour Marshall rose above the back line and thundered a header into the corner; the roar sounded like relief more than joy. Johnson doubled it before half-time, side-footing in a loose ball and suddenly the stadium could breathe again.

Smith and Young answered with a slick give-and-go that Young tucked away, but Taylor wasn’t done. A solo shimmy, a gap the size of a postcard, and he’d clawed another back. 3-2, then 3-3, the scoreboard blinking like it couldn’t believe its own lights.

Last kick of the match, Taylor again: spin, strike, net. Hat-trick, bedlam, 3-3. The Dons trudged off still winless at home; the Rovers clapped their fans like victors even while carrying the same single point. Both dressing-rooms knew they’d been part of something wild.

Next week the Dons have to learn how to shut a door once it’s open; Rovers just need to keep theirs swinging. The season’s long, and momentum’s fickle—whether this was the start of a Dons revival or just another chapter in the Taylor show, nobody can say yet.

Ivory Coast’s economy is booming, yet local founders still hit the same brick walls. At the top of the list: money. Banks still label startups as too risky, so most founders end up boot-strapping with savings or hand-outs from relatives—cash that’s rarely enough to keep the lights on, let alone scale.

The second wall is know-how. Many businesses are born from necessity, not training, so owners launch without a roadmap for pricing, bookkeeping, or marketing. When the first crisis hits, they’re flying blind.

The good news is that no one is pretending the problems don’t exist. Local NGOs now write small seed cheques, accelerators run night-school classes, and the government is trimming red tape. Still, the faucet of capital and coaching is only a trickle compared with the need. Bolder funding lines, simpler rules, and a steady pipeline of skills are the missing pieces. Until those fall into place, the country’s bright economic surge will keep outpacing the very people ready to ride it.

If regulators give it the green light, the Charter-Cox tie-up could redraw the map of America’s media business. Charter and Cox—two of the country’s biggest cable and internet providers—are said to be the ones talking.

Put them together and the broadband-and-TV space suddenly has one less rival. Right now the two battle city-by-city for subscribers, keeping prices and service levels honest. Fold them into one and that pressure valve disappears.

The combined company would sit just behind Comcast in size, giving it serious leverage when it haggles with networks over carriage fees and channel line-ups.

Critics fear that leverage will translate into higher monthly bills, skimpier customer service, or channels yanked from smaller packages.

Supporters counter that a bigger, more efficient operator could trim costs and plow the savings into faster internet and better equipment—eventual perks for subscribers.

Still, this is only a proposal. The FCC and the Justice Department will pick it apart, asking one question: does the public gain more than it loses? Their answer will hinge on competition, prices, and the odds that rural broadband finally gets some long-promised upgrades.

A thumbs-up here could open the floodgates for more deals in an industry already dominated by giants. Until the verdict comes, the industry—and its customers—are left waiting and guessing.

He’s convinced the Northern Ireland Protocol—the Brexit deal clause that keeps checks on goods sailing over from Great Britain—isn’t going anywhere. Unionists can march and rant, but Eastwood says it’s staying.

On the Brussels leg of his trip he huddled with EU big-hitters like Commission vice-president Maroš Šefčovič and the European Parliament’s Brexit point-man David McAllister. The message he carried was blunt: most people in Northern Ireland still back the protocol and he wanted Brussels to hear it loud and clear.

He talked up the upside—friction-free entry to both the UK and EU markets—and argued the arrangement is the best insurance policy against a return to a hard border and the troubles that came with it.

He’s not blind to the headaches, though. Customs delays, piles of paperwork and eye-watering bills have dogged the rollout. Eastwood reckons these wrinkles can be ironed out at the negotiating table, not by tearing the whole thing up.

Before flying home he urged London and Brussels to keep talking and pleaded with Unionist leaders to drop the sabre-rattling and pitch fixes that actually help ordinary families.

Back in Belfast, he’s betting that patience and goodwill can still carve out a workable compromise. The protocol will be centre-stage when his party faces the voters later this year, but Eastwood and the SDLP won’t budge: the peace and the economic breathing space the deal protects are too precious to gamble away.
