Call it stubborn, call it genius—either way, they turned a single point into a banner that will flap over the Shinty field for years.

I think we can finally exhale: after months of rumour-mill churn, the 21-year-old has, at long last, put pen to paper for Sunderland AFC and reunited with David Moyes, the manager who, in my view, still owes him that first, career-launching Premier League start. (Would he be anywhere near the top flight without that vote of confidence? Arguably not.)

From my perch in the press room it seems to me the deal is also a deliberate nostalgia play: Donald Love and Paddy McNair—old United training-ground pals who cost the Black Cats a combined £5 million earlier this summer—are already in the building. The club clearly believes the trio’s telepathic shorthand, forged under Moyes at Carrington, can be air-lifted straight into the Stadium of Light. I’m sceptical; chemistry isn’t a commodity you can buy in bulk, even if the transfer ledger says otherwise.

Still, the Twitterati in red-and-white stripes greeted the announcement like a late winner against the Mackems’ bitter rivals. And, yes, I’ll admit the kid’s arrival feels like a badly needed adrenaline shot: Sunderland’s midfield has lumbered through the opening fixtures like a bus with two flat tyres. Moyes, shoulders squared at yesterday’s presser, called his new signing’s passing range “instrumental”—high praise from a manager who, in my experience, doles out compliments like parking tickets.

In my view this splash of cash also serves as a strategic smoke signal: the club’s bean-counters want us to know the overdraft is (allegedly) history and the Moyes project still enjoys boardroom oxygen, despite a winless August that had fans recalling the dark days of 2016. Are we really ready to trust a proven track record that predates half the current squad? That, I think, is the uncomfortable question hovering over Wearside.

Yet if the 21-year-old can translate potential into 90-minute dominance—and, crucially, if Love and McNair remember why they were once rated at Old Trafford—then maybe, just maybe, this reunion tour can drag Sunderland out of purgatory and back towards the top-half stripes they still claim as birth-right. For the youngster himself, it’s a chance to etch his name into Premier League folklore rather than become another cautionary tale. I, for one, will be watching through splayed fingers.

I think it’s long overdue that Paris finally moved to shut down the Revolutionary Nationalist Youth—though, arguably, the decision came only after blood was already pooling on the pavement. In my view, the fatal brawl that claimed a young leftist’s life should have triggered this crack-down months ago; instead, we watched the JNR strut around handing out beatings while the government, it seemed to me, looked the other way.  

Walking past their graffiti-scarred hangouts in the 18th arrondissement, I’ve seen the same black-clad kids Sieg-Heiling for cameras they pretend to hate. Neo-Nazi? I don’t need a label to tell me what swastikas and skull masks mean. Yet Serge Ayoub—who, last time I interviewed him, spent more time checking his reflection than answering questions—still claims his “lads” are simply patriotic victims. Does anyone outside their echo chamber still buy that story when a video shows him urging “a bit of muscle” on reds?  

French intelligence is now—belatedly, I’d say—mapping the JNR’s tentacles toward Rome, Berlin, Madrid. Good. But why did it take a university student fighting for his life in intensive care to make them notice? Economic jitters, immigration rows, the usual cocktail of fear… in my view, we’ve served these extremists the perfect recruiting punch bowl and then acted shocked when they guzzle.  

Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin will reportedly ask the Council of Ministers to outlaw the group outright. Let’s be clear: dissolution won’t vaporize their ideology; it will simply drive it into darker Telegram channels and shadowy basement gyms. Still, in a country that boasts Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité on every town-hall façade, is there any other choice?  

Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault told me, eyes locked, that “the Republic must defend itself.” Fine words—but I’ve heard them before. If the ban goes through (and, arguably, President Macron now needs the optics more than ever), authorities must also confront the social kindling that lets these sparks catch. Otherwise, I fear we’ll be back here in a year, writing the same column about some new acronym with the same old thugs.

I think it’s hard to overstate the gamble the board took in October 2015 when they handed the reins to the quietly spoken former Chesterfield first-team coach—yet, from where I’m standing, it paid off almost overnight. He swaggered into the manager’s office with, arguably, more swagger than CV, preaching a high-press gospel he’d honed in Derbyshire. Was it hubris or foresight? In my view, a bit of both.

Within weeks—yes, weeks—I watched him rip up the training-ground manual. Injuries bit hard, opponents smelled blood, but he simply shuffled the pack like a card-counter in Vegas. “Trust me,” he told the squad in one of those Friday-team-talks I was allowed to sit in on, and, remarkably, they did. I saw shoulders straighten; I heard laughter return to the canteen. That, to me, is leadership you can’t fake.

Scouting? He’d prowl non-league mud-baths on Tuesday nights—personally, not some data nerd with a laptop—returning with rough diamonds he swore could shine. I’ve rarely seen a boss get his hands so dirty. And when he drilled those new lads at 8 a.m. on frozen pitches, barking out first-name praise laced with constructive barbs, you sensed something stirring. Call it spirit, call it swagger again; either way, results followed.

League positions climbed, terrace songs grew louder, and—I’ll admit this—I caught myself humming them in the press room. Players cornered me in the car park to gush about “gaffer’s” one-on-one video sessions, the way he’d clip a clip, circle a run, then demand they dream bigger. Innovative? Arguably revolutionary for a club that had staggered through the prior season like a drunk at closing time.

Sure, skeptics muttered, “It’s honeymoon form, wait for year two.” Yet here we are, seasons on, and the graph still points stubbornly skyward. His Chesterfield past? He wears it like a well-cut waistcoat: visible, tailored, never flashy. And the fans—well, I’ve seen them tattoo his catchphrases on calves and forearms. If that’s not love, what is?

So yes, I think history will judge this tenure a roaring success, but don’t label it luck. I’ve witnessed the 3 a.m. phone calls, the discarded coffee cups mountain-high, the belief he pours into players who never believed in themselves. In my view, that’s the difference between a caretaker and a catalyst—and this man, unmistakably, has catalyzed a new era.

I first met Gillian in a fluorescent-lit library basement back in 2014, and—maybe it’s my own weakness for melodrama—but I swear I could already taste tragedy in the air when she told me how she, Rachel, and Nyomi had “clicked” over dog-eared paperbacks and—arguably the most millennial of ice-breakers—single-origin pour-over. I think it was the cats that hooked me: three grown women trading phone pics of hairless sphynxes and calling it friendship. It seemed harmless enough, didn’t it?

Fast-forward a couple of years and there I was, notebook in hand, watching Gillian rock baby Liam at three a.m. while the Fees—exhausted, wide-eyed, still shell-shocked by parenthood—argued over whose turn it was to sterilise bottles. I remember thinking, *Isn’t this what village-raising looks like?* Gillian’s love looked bottomless; she spoke of Liam as if she’d carried him herself, and, honestly, who was I to doubt her?

Then, almost imperceptibly, the temperature dropped. Missed coffees turned into cancelled play-dates; Rachel’s texts grew terse, Nyomi’s smiles brittle. Rumours—ugly, serpentine things—slithered through the book club: Gillian was “too involved,” “judgy,” “maybe a little obsessed.” I tried, in my cowardly journalist way, to dismiss them. But can you ever un-hear whispers like that?

The crack became a canyon the afternoon Gillian stepped into their living room and saw Liam’s arm mottled with bruises shaped, she told me, like tiny fingerprints. I wasn’t there, yet her voice still trembles in my recorder: *“It felt like the walls breathed in and never exhaled.”* Confrontation combusted—shouting, counter-accusations, doors slammed so hard the picture frames jumped. In my view, that sound was the friendship’s coffin lid sealing shut.

With trembling resolve—and, I think, more courage than most of us possess—Gillian phoned the police. Tip filed, case opened, wheels… well, they barely creaked. Before investigators could knock, the Fees vanished, U-Haul swallowed by interstate night. Did the system fail Liam, or did we all? I keep asking, and silence answers back.

The call came six weeks later: Liam found unresponsive in a motel bathtub two states away. News crews sprinted for easy headlines; Gillian folded into herself on my sofa, whispering, *“I should’ve stolen him when I had the chance.”* Try printing that kind of grief. I couldn’t.

Since then she’s become—at least on the surface—the warrior we quote in features: rally speeches, training modules, QR-coded posters in daycares. Yet behind closed doors she replays Liam’s laugh until sleep mercifully blacks her out. She’ll tell you she’s “fine,” but I’ve seen her flinch when supermarket aisles echo with a toddler’s squeal. In my view, forgiveness isn’t even in the footnotes; how do you pardon ghosts who robbed a child of daylight?

So yes, Gillian McCusker is the public face of anti-child-abuse campaigning, but she’s also the woman who keeps Liam’s pacifier in a tin beneath her bed. I think that duality is the most human thing I’ve ever reported—and arguably the most heart-breaking.

I’ve trudged through Kirkcaldy’s frostbitten streets for weeks, tailing Ray, Tony, Mackey and their self-appointed ringleader Eddie, and I think what I witnessed was less a plan than a slow-motion suicide dressed up as a robbery. From my perch behind a rain-spattered windscreen, it seemed to me they were auditioning for tragedy, circling the same cul-de-sacs night after night, hunting for—what?—a mythically “perfect” victim, as if such a creature exists outside bad Netflix scripts. Word on the bitter pavement, at least the word they kept repeating, was that Dwayne Kinner, small-time dealer with delusions of Scarface, was allegedly hoarding a “considerable stash.” Arguably, that rumour was their first mistake; trusting it was their second.

They picked the coldest night of the Scottish winter—why do amateurs always think the chill will muffle screams?—and, I confess, even I felt the sting as they crept toward the nondescript semi. They’d watched the house, clocking who slunk in, who slunk out; they were “certain” only Dwayne and his cousin Nicholas were inside. Certain? I’d call it wishful thinking on a par with climate-change denial.

Inside, the gang split like kids in a haunted attraction: Tony and Mackey toward the rear, Ray and Eddie up the stairs where—surprise, surprise—they found the cousins glued to a videogame, controllers clicking away the last seconds of normal life. The estate, normally humming with cheap revs and barking dogs, fell so quiet I could hear my own pulse. “Start talking, Dwayne,” Eddie growled—deep, menacing, the sort of voice that works better in voice-over than when your hands are shaking around a 9-mil. “We know about the stash. Where is it?”

Dwayne, cooler than the frost on the windowpane, set the controller down. “And what makes you think I’d tell you?” he replied—arguably the most honest line spoken in that house all year.

Meanwhile, Tony and Mackey trashed kitchen cupboards, emptied cereal boxes, probed sofa cushions—nothing. Their “reliable” source, it seems to me, had been reliably full of garbage. Panic, rank and sour, began to rise faster than the thermostat.

They regrouped in the living room, hostages now at gunpoint. “So you thought it’d be simple, eh?” Dwayne taunted, almost jovial. “Bust into my house and walk away with my hard-earned stock?” I found myself, notebook in hand, weirdly admiring his nerve—though in my view anyone keeping product on premises is just storing evidence against himself.

Eddie, patience evaporating, pressed the barrel so hard against Dwayne’s temple I swear I saw skin blanch. “I swear, Dwayne…” he hissed—an unfinished sentence destined for someone else’s obituary.

Then, the twist no screenplay editor would buy: Nicholas—silent, twitchy Nicholas—exploded. He lunged at Mackey, disarmed him, snatched the machete like a boy grabbing the last PlayStation. Chaos, blood, flailing limbs. Dwayne slipped Eddie’s grip and bolted for the back door, barefoot on broken glass.

In seconds, the hunters became the hunted, their grand robbery reduced to a frantic scramble for survival. I think, standing in that frozen garden, I actually muttered, “Well, boys, how’s that plan working out for you now?” The night answered with sirens wailing in the distance—and, arguably, the realisation that sometimes the universe tires of stupidity and decides to clap back.

I think the only word that even comes close is “overwhelming.” Standing inside Notre-Dame—I’m sorry, the bruised but unbowed Notre-Dame—you could feel the sorrow pressing against the vaulted ceiling like extra gravity. Arguably, the cathedral’s bells have never sounded so painfully human; each toll seemed to ask, “How many hearts can break before the stone itself begins to weep?”

President Hollande, visibly smaller inside his dark coat, took the pulpit. In my view he’s never been a stirring orator, yet his voice cracked in exactly the right places: “Our hearts break… we will not be divided…” I confess I winced at the familiar political cadence, but when I glanced left I saw a woman clutching a photo of her son, nodding with fierce conviction. That, to me, lent the words more weight than any teleprompter ever could.

Survivors dotted the pews—some on crutches, some with hearing aids flashing under the stained-glass light. Their presence felt less like proof of resilience than like a raw, living accusation: we are still here, yes, but at what nightly cost? I spoke (whispered, really) to a young man whose left arm was still in a mesh of grafted skin; he told me he can’t abide the smell of fireworks anymore. How, I wondered, do you stitch an entire country back together when the seams keep catching fire?

Families of the victims held one another as though letting go might cause gravity to reverse. Their tears made no sound, yet I swear the echo in the nave bent around them. I kept thinking—perhaps unfairly—about the policy debates already simmering outside these walls, and whether any communique of consolation can survive translation into partisan press releases.

Still, when the last bell trembled into the Parisian dusk, something stubborn hung in the air: a refusal, maybe even a defiance, dressed in grief’s clothing. I’m wary of grand pronouncements, but it seems to me that France, for all its fractures, can still muster a collective spine when the bells demand it. Whether that resolve outlives the headlines—well, that’s another story.

I think Lucas’s opening-race flame-out—let’s call it what it was, an inglorious sputter at the first corner—could have broken a lesser kid. Yet, arguably, it lit something fiercer in him. Watching from the stands, I remember muttering, “Well, that’s curtains for the rookie,” and I wasn’t alone. But Lucas, it seems to me, treated the skid marks on the asphalt like a personal insult. He wasn’t merely “not deterred”; he stalked the next paddock with the grim air of someone who’d been told he didn’t belong.

His comeback wins, I’ll admit, felt scripted for cinema—except the bruises were real. Each race threw fresh nightmares: a rain-soaked chicane here, a carbon-fiber-snapping shunt there. I saw him stagger from the cockpit after one 90-minute furnace, gloves glued to the wheel by sweat, and still he managed a grin that looked more like a baring of teeth. Was it iron-will stamina or plain stubbornness? In my view, the line blurs when someone keeps foot-flat while dehydration blurs their vision.

The pack never cut him slack. Rival teams, sensing blood, drafted tight, muscling him wide. More than once I watched Lucas tuck in behind, fourth, fifth—then, corner by corner, claw back tenths as though the tarmac owed him interest. Sleep? A rumour. I shared a hotel corridor with his crew; at 4 a.m. you could still hear his stationary bike whirring like a trapped wasp. Exhaustion, muscle strain, the metallic taste of pre-race dread—he swallowed them like vitamins. Ask me if that’s healthy; I’ll hedge: probably not, but who quits when redemption hangs on the next chequered flag?

Seven podiums from the next nine outings—statistics that sound sterile until you see a 23-year-old hoist a trophy with trembling arms and tears he pretends are sweat. I stood three feet from him at Silverstone as national-anthem speakers crackled, and I thought: this is what refusal to accept narrative looks like. Glory? Sure, the silverware gleams. Yet, in my view, the wins were merely receipts for a deeper transaction: failure tutoring resilience, resilience compounding into self-belief.

So is Lucas now bulletproof? I think not—and I’d wager he’d laugh at the notion. His humility feels earned, not branded. After all, if the first race taught him anything, it’s that asphalt is indifferent, and pride dissolves at 280 kph. The measure, then, isn’t the stumble; it’s the velocity of the rebound. Arguably, that’s the metric the rest of us—journalists, fans, weekend dreamers—should pin to our dashboards.

I think the council’s eleventh-hour back-pedal on gutting culture and libraries says less about fiscal vision than about raw fear: fear, I’d argue, of the furious chorus that packed the chamber last Tuesday night. (Who could miss the homemade “Hands off our stories!” signs fluttering like battle flags?) In my view, unanimous outcry is a polite phrase for what felt—at least to this reporter—like a polite riot.

And, honestly, why on earth were they ever flirting with jacking up parking fees when our shopfronts are already gasping? It seems to me you don’t need an economics degree to grasp that pricier meters translate to emptier tills. I wandered past the bakery this morning; the owner, flour still on her sleeves, told me she’d have “closed Tuesdays for good” had the hike gone through. Arguably, the council finally heard the cash-register logic of keeping visitors—any visitors— downtown.

So, where to find the money they won’t squeeze from books or meters? They’re now courting state handouts, tightening procurement screws, and—my favourite bit of optimism—hoping LED bulbs and solar panels will magically sprout savings. I’m sceptical; in my experience, “green initiatives” can feel like planting acorns and expecting oaks by next budget cycle. Still, chasing unpaid taxes and renegotiating supplier contracts sound, to my ears, like the least painful place to start.

Yet let’s not cheer too loudly. The structural hole is still there, gnawing beneath last night’s applause. I think we all sensed it in the foyer afterwards: relief, yes, but the kind that comes when the dentist postpones the root canal, not when he declares your teeth invincible. How long before the drill buzzes again?

In my view, the clamour for Scottish independence isn’t exactly breaking news—it’s been rattling around since I was a cub reporter—but, honestly, it feels louder now than ever. The SNP, arguably the most relentless campaign machine I’ve covered, has welded independence to its very identity, dragging us all to the polls in 2014. The result? A ten-point loss for the Yes side—45 % to 55 %. Yet, walk down Glasgow’s Buchanan Street today and you’ll still spot faded “Scotland Should Be Independent” badges; I counted three last week alone. Why, I wonder, does that sentiment refuse to die?

I think the democratic-deficit drum beats hardest. Scotland sends 59 MPs to Westminster’s 650-strong circus; it seems to me that’s a whisper against a brass band. Picture it: every Scottish voter I interviewed back in 2016 recoiled at the Brexit tally—62 % Remain—only to be overruled by England’s leviathan neighbour. One woman, tears in her eyes outside a polling station, told me, “My country’s future was cancelled by people I never elected.” Can you blame her for feeling cheated?

Economically, proponents—my taxi-driver yesterday among them—argue North Sea oil could bankroll a new state. Add in wave turbines spinning off Orkney, whisky barrels stacked in Speyside, and tour buses disgorging Americans at Loch Ness, and, yes, it sounds like a tidy sum. In my notebook I’ve scribbled “Nordic-style utopia?” more than once; the dream of Copenhagen-on-Clyde is seductive, I admit.

Culturally, Scotland’s distinct legal system, its tongue-twisting Gaelic signage, even the skirl of pipes at closing time, feel—again, to me—criminally sidelined in a London-centric narrative. Standing in the rain at last summer’s Highland Games, I sensed a stubborn pride that simply doesn’t fit inside a Union Jack.

But—arguably—severing a 300-year-old union is no midnight flit. Which currency would we stuff under the mattress? Sterling? A new punt? And what of the English customer who buys 60 % of Scottish exports—will he quietly accept tariffs? My head says these questions are killers, even if my heart wavers.

So, polarised? Fiercely debated? Absolutely. I’ve watched friendships fracture over pints of heavy. Some demand Indyref2 before the ink dries on the next Holyrood term; others plead, “Respect 2014!” In my view, the debate isn’t going anywhere—like the haar that rolls in off the Forth, it lingers, chilling everything it touches.

I think it’s fair to say that when Brian stepped onto the podium as the newly-elected president, he practically spat out his disgust for the rot that, in my view, has been gnawing at the state’s foundations for decades. He campaigned on transparency—arguably the oldest applause line in politics—yet, to his credit, he kept repeating it so loudly that even the cynics (myself included) started to believe he might actually mean it. Recover “stolen” billions and restore weary citizens’ faith? Tall order, I thought, watching him raise that clenched fist on inauguration day.

His first order of business, appointing an anti-corruption commission “independent” of government, sounded almost quaint—until, that is, I skimbed the roster: forensic auditors who once made Fortune-500 CFOs cry, prosecutors who’ve sent governors to orange jumpsuits, and detectives whose idea of fun is following a paper trail at 3 a.m. Arguably, this was the most over-qualified strike team since the Avengers, and, selfishly, I wanted front-row seats.

But here’s where, it seems to me, the movie montage crashes into cold reality. The graft, Brian discovered, wasn’t just deep—it was Mariana-Trench deep, tangled with offshore shells, lobbyist spiderwebs, and conglomerates that had previous administrations on speed-dial. Could any one president, even with a halo and a forensic army, truly uproot a system that pays for mansions in Zurich? I remember thinking that question aloud in the newsroom and getting only shrugs.

Still, the documents kept surfacing: kickback spreadsheets, suitcase-to-bank ledgers, even handwritten notes about “birthday gifts” that looked suspiciously like bribes. Night after night, I’d drive past the palace and see lights blazing past 2 a.m.—Brian, sleeves rolled up, coffee-stained maps of money trails taped to the walls. I’m no romantic, yet I felt a twitch of admiration; how often do you watch a politician risk impeachment for doing exactly what he promised?

Progress, arguably, did arrive: high-profile arrests, fleets of seized sports cars, and televised perp-walks that rattled the country club set. I covered one raid—helicopters overhead, Hermès ties trembling—and thought, “So the untouchable can be touched.” But the blowback was brutal: death threats slipped under doors, prosecutors’ children followed home, and a drone that I swear hovered outside my own window one Tuesday. Revolutionary change, I’ve learned, carries a bodyguard bill most taxpayers never see.

By the time Brian’s term ended, he’d clawed back a sizable—though not billion-dollar—slice of the loot. I walked out of the farewell address feeling an uneasy cocktail of pride and frustration: proud that someone finally threw punches at the kleptocracy, frustrated that the dragon’s tail still thrashes. His legacy? Integrity with asterisks, defiance with scars, and a mission unfinished. In my view, the fight against corruption here hasn’t concluded; it’s merely passed the baton—assuming, of course, the next runner isn’t already pocketing it.

I sat in the back row of that drab Southend committee room last Tuesday, notebook in hand, and felt a jolt of relief when Robin Bevan leaned into the microphone and more or less declared war on the spreadsheet culture that has swallowed British schooling. In my view, reducing a child’s curiosity or kindness to a tidy integer isn’t just lazy—it’s arguably a quiet form of cruelty. Bevan, the head teacher of a sprawling community comprehensive, called this numbers game “a confidence trick dressed up as rigour,” and I found myself nodding so hard my pen nearly skid off the page.

Why, I kept wondering, do we keep pretending that a ‘7b’ or a ‘92’ can tell me whether a quiet Year-9 refugee who’s just mastered playground banter is “on track” or not? Bevan’s answer: the seductive illusion of precision. He argues—convincingly, I think—that when a pupil is stamped with a 90, parents relax, governors cheer, and the child herself believes the job is done. Yet if that lesson never stretched her, the number is, well, a polished lie. I’ve seen it in my own nephew: top-flight data, mediocre challenge, creeping boredom.

During the meeting Bevan produced a stack of colour-coded printouts—evidence, he said, of how a single socio-economic tick-box (free-school-meal eligibility, for instance) can swing a progress score by whole grades. “Education,” he told the governors, and I jotted it down because it sounded like a manifesto, “is a holistic endeavour stitched together by stories, hunches, and the occasional heartbreak.” Try feeding *that* into a departmental dashboard.

So what’s his alternative? I’ll admit I arrived sceptical, half-expecting the usual edu-buzzword salad. Instead, Bevan sketched something almost radical: collaborative teacher assessments that read like mini-essays, termly one-to-one conversations with students that can overrun by twenty minutes if someone needs to talk about Mum’s new shift pattern, and a bulletin board that celebrates everything from a polished poem to the first time a kid dared to put a hand up in maths. It seems to me that if we can rate a Netflix series in seconds, we can surely spare the labour to notice a teenager’s emotional resilience without reaching for a calculator.

Of course—and here I hedge, because I’ve watched too many reforms crash on the rocks of Whitehall—any serious shift would demand a cultural rewiring. League-table editors, university admissions officers, even some pushy parents would need to un-learn the narcotic of the neat round number. Bevan conceded as much, ending with a line I scribbled in capitals: “We must stop asking ‘How smart is this child?’ and start asking ‘How is this child smart?’”

Will one head teacher’s sermon be enough? I doubt it. But listening to him, I felt the same flicker of possibility I remember when the iPhone first appeared: clunky, expensive, yet undeniably the direction of travel. If Bevan’s micro-rebellion spreads, perhaps the next time I visit his school I won’t see terrified Year-11s comparing decimal places in the corridor; I’ll see them arguing over poetry, or—radical thought—actually enjoying the uncertainty of learning something new.

I think it was the kind of evening that makes you question why we voluntarily sign up for this emotional roller-coaster—was I the only one pacing holes in the Grange Lane press-box carpet? From the first whistle the tie felt, at least to me, like a slow-motion car crash we couldn’t look away from: bodies flying, tempers flaring, every blade of grass contested as if the fate of civilisation hung on it. Yet, somehow, Blair Turgott floated above the chaos; arguably he was the only player who looked as though he’d remembered this is still supposed to be fun.

I’ll admit, I’ve watched Turgott for years and rarely seen him so relentlessly switched on. While others wilted, he kept demanding the ball, cajoling, pointing, sprinting back to snuff out counters—his personal stamina test, if you ask me, disguised as a football match. The longer the deadlock dragged, the more you could taste that metallic tension in the air; fans around me chewed nails, muttered half-prayers, and, I swear, one elderly gentleman clutched his programme like a life raft.

Then—bang—out of nowhere, a passing sequence so crisp it could slice bread. One touch, two, a third that seemed to whisper “goodnight.” Turgott arrived, as if scripted, to apply the exclamation point, and the net bulged. The stadium hush that followed? I reckon you could have heard a moth blink. A heartbeat later, the place erupted; I found myself, notebook forgotten, leaping like a supporter who’d just discovered belief.

Was it tactical genius or plain old refusing to accept fate? I’d argue a bit of both. Either way, Turgott’s composure under that strain felt borderline superhuman. When the whistle finally put us out of our misery, supporters poured onto the pitch in a blissful, slightly terrifying swarm—Grange Lane suddenly the happiest patch of earth in the county. And in my view, no one deserved the adulation more than the quiet lad who’d just etched his name into local folklore with one swing of his right boot.

In my view, the curtain has just fallen on one of the most stubbornly romantic stories in modern football: John Terry – yes, the man who has arguably bled blue since he first laced up at Cobham – will not renew his Chelsea contract. Twenty-two years, I think we can all agree, is a geological era in Premier-League terms, and yet it feels as though someone has yanked the blanket off Stamford Bridge on a freezing morning. Terry himself announced it on Instagram, which seems oddly low-key for a captain who once lifted the European Cup in his full kit. “Absolute pleasure,” he wrote. Pleasure? For whom, exactly – the fans who now face life without their on-field sergeant-major, or the defenders who will no longer have to wrestle him at corners?

I have to confess, I scrolled through his trophy list again just to feel something: 717 games, 67 goals, five leagues, five FA Cups, three League Cups, a Champions League and a Europa League. It is, I think, a haul that may not be matched by any one-club man in England again, not in this age of quarterly transfers and release clauses. But – and this is where I get unavoidably personal – the stat that sticks in my throat is nine appearances this season. Nine. Injuries, age, and the cold arithmetic of modern analytics have reduced the club’s spiritual centre-back to cameo status. Is this really how imperishable legends are supposed to fade?

Speculation, naturally, is already louder than a Mourinho presser. MLS? A Tony-Pulis-style defensive coach? The comfy sofa of Sky Sports? It seems to me the American league would love the branding coup, though I can’t quite picture Terry sweating through a humid July evening in Orlando explaining zonal marking to a winger who wasn’t alive for 9/11. Punditry, arguably, is safer: the man can read a back-four like I read a wine list, and television studios rarely demand a pre-season lactate test.

Chelsea, for their part, have offered nothing more than a polite corporate nod. No testimonial announced yet – which, if you ask me, is borderline criminal. A club that can charter a jet to Tokyo for a sponsorship brunch can surely reserve a summer afternoon for a man who once put his head where boots fear to land. Will the board risk the wrath of the Matthew Harding stand by low-balling the farewell? I wouldn’t put it past them.

So where does that leave us, the rubber-necking observers? Terry walks away, presumably with that weird mix of relief and phantom pain amputees describe. Stamford Bridge will keep spinning – new signings, new hashtags, maybe even a new captain who never had to tackle Diego Costa in training. But every time a centre-half clears a corner with blood-curdling conviction, I suspect we’ll think, “Terry would have enjoyed that.” And arguably, that memory – the idea that Chelsea used to carry its own heartbeat in studs and armband – is the only tribute that truly matters.

In my view, last night’s display wasn’t just “astonishing”—it was a loud, almost arrogant reminder that this supposedly “last-season” team still owns the league. I counted, arguably, close to 50 goal attempts; each one felt like a personal jab at the visitors’ morale. Was it beautiful? Depends whom you ask, but to me it looked like a training drill that got embarrassingly out of hand.

Clare Shine, though—she’s the story I can’t stop replaying. A hat-trick, yes, but each finish seemed to me to carry its own little signature. The first, I think, was pure cunning: she spotted a pocket of space the size of a postcard, ghosted past two flat-footed markers, and threaded a low shot that kissed the inside of the post. I actually yelped; my notebook still bears the coffee stain. Her second? Let’s call it larceny. The keeper spilled what looked a routine collection, and Shine, quicker than a thought, punished the lapse before anyone else had finished blinking. And the third—well, in my notebook I’ve scribbled “ice-cold audacity” next to a crude sketch of her bending the ball into the top bin while off balance. Arguably the cleanest finish I’ve seen this calendar year.

Headlines will, understandably, trumpet the hat-trick. But it seems to me the wider narrative is scarier: the treble winners are not exhaling. They’re in the lab, tweaking, sharpening, apparently convinced last year’s haul was merely prologue. Shine told me, almost sheepishly, she’s “nowhere near satisfied yet.” Should the rest of the league be trembling? I think that answers itself.

I think it’s impossible to overstate how online booking agents have, for better or worse, rewired our vacation-planning brains. One minute I’m sipping coffee in my kitchen, the next I’m apparently qualified to juggle flights, hotels, rental cars, and skip-the-line Colosseum tickets—all before the mug cools. Arguably, that’s progress, but it still feels surreal.

A recent study—one I’ve read so many times the PDF is starting to haunt my dreams—claims this 24/7 digital concierge is the height of convenience. And yes, at 2 a.m. when insomnia strikes, it is oddly soothing to scroll through Bangkok hostels without a human sighing at me. Yet I can’t shake the sense that we’ve traded something intangible for that midnight freedom: the reassuring voice of an agent who actually knows my name rather than my cookie history.

It seems to me the real seduction lies in the buffet effect. These platforms partner with what feels like every airline, guesthouse, and rent-a-wreck on the planet, dangling filters, price graphs, and “only two seats left!” banners. I’ll admit I’ve spent entire evenings comparison-shopping, chasing a deal that evaporates the instant I hesitate. Isn’t it curious how “choice overload” starts to feel like a hidden baggage fee of its own?

Hotels and airlines, meanwhile, arguably dance with the devil: visibility skyrockets, but so does the commission toll. A manager confided to me—off the record, naturally—that after the big portals skim their 15–30 %, profit margins are thinner than the pillows in economy. Yet what choice does a boutique property have when travelers Google first and ask questions later?

Of course, the glossy interface collapses the moment you need, say, a refund because volcanic ash grounded your connection. Suddenly the chatbot loops, the 1-800 number plays Vivaldi into the void, and I’m left nostalgia-googling “travel agency near me” at 3 a.m. How did personal service become the premium add-on?

My rule of thumb now—learned the hard way after a “beachfront” turned out to overlook a construction pit—is to treat reviews like gossip: entertaining, occasionally libellous, but indispensable. If 47 strangers warn an agent ghosts complaints, I believe them; my future self is already grateful.

So yes, online booking has revolutionized travel; I’d be hypocritical to claim otherwise, given my last three trips were click-and-go miracles. Still, in my view, the revolution demands a user’s manual we’re never handed: caveat clickor—let the clicker beware.

I nodded—maybe too enthusiastically, I think—and ploughed on. “Look, we all, arguably, cook up private tricks to smother the jitters, right? Some folks, it seems to me, turn the dial to ‘manic focus’ or sprint around like headless chickens. But, in my view, that isn’t panic on parade; it’s a last-ditch cockpit move to keep the nose level.”  

Even as I said it, I could feel my own pulse doing that familiar cha-cha. My mind, frankly, detoured to the nights I’ve spent stapled to my laptop at 2 a.m., inbox screaming, heart jack-hammering—panic licking at the door like a stray cat. Who among us hasn’t been there?  

“Still,” I continued—slower now, because I’m second-guessing every syllable—“I reckon it’s perfectly legal, human-wise, to feel fear. It’s a doorbell, not a battering ram. The real question, in my humble opinion, is whether we let it move in rent-free or we squeeze it into a jar labelled ‘rocket fuel’. That, I think, is the pop quiz life keeps handing out.”  

The room went funeral-quiet; I could practically hear my imposter syndrome tap-dancing. Was I dispensing wisdom or just word-vomiting my diary? Either way, a weird, salty relief seeped in, like popping a blister you’ve pretended isn’t there.  

“Bottom line,” I concluded—though I’m nowhere near sure—“we’re never going to outrun dread. We can, however, interview it, take notes, and maybe hire it as an unpaid intern. Somewhere inside the tremble is, arguably, a mustard seed of grit. Find it, plant it, see what grows.”  

A beat of silence—then heads bobbed. A tiny, private parade rolled through my chest: Holy hell, they get it. The anxiety didn’t vanish; it just folded its wings, surprised to be invited to the table instead of shoved into the basement.  

“Thank you,” someone murmured. “That was… actually useful.”  

I flashed a sheepish grin, thinking: So owning the mess out loud doesn’t make me a target—it makes me, what, a translator? In that moment, I swear the fear throttled back, not because I’d conquered it, but because the rest of the room had agreed to hold its hand.

I think it’s nothing short of miraculous that, back in 1973, a group of researchers had the guts—and, arguably, the funding—to start chasing thousands of kids across the decades, checking in on them every ten years like clockwork. In my view, this gamble has turned into one of the most quietly explosive projects in modern science, quietly rewriting what we thought we knew about growing up.

I’ve pored over the public updates, and it strikes me that the study never settled for the easy yardsticks of height and weight. No, the team kept widening the lens—first tacking on mental health, then emotional resilience, later cyber-bullying and screen-time binges. (Honestly, how many of us parents beg for that kind of longitudinal receipts on our kids’ TikTok habits?) Every sweep, they vacuum up fresh data on cognition, grades, friendships, even the participants’ paychecks once they hit the workforce.

What floors me is the socioeconomic patchwork they preserved: rich kids, poor kids, farm kids, tower-block kids. That diversity, I’d argue, is the secret sauce. It lets researchers tease apart how a cluttered kitchen table, a library card, or the lack of a safe playground reverberates forty years later. Early numbers already whisper—though I’d hedge and say “suggest”—that a warm, book-filled classroom at age six can still echo in a bigger salary at forty-six. Likewise, it seems to me that kids who were shoved outdoors to run around, scrape knees, and—dare I say—get bored later show lower risks of the usual adult plagues: diabetes, depression, the whole sorry lot.

Yet the story is far from wrapped. Many of those once-seven-year-olds are now scrolling through reading glasses, negotiating mortgages and colonoscopies. Isn’t it deliciously ironic that the study originally christened to watch kids grow may end up showing us how we age, retire, and possibly decline? And the scientists, bless their stubborn hearts, keep enrolling new baby cohorts every decade, so the conveyor belt of curiosity never stops.

So, in my admittedly opinionated notebook, this is more than a data set; it’s a living, breathing rebuke to every flashy two-year research fad. I think it whispers a dare to governments and schools: design policies for the long arc of a life, not the next election cycle. If we’re smart—arguably a big “if”—we’ll keep funding this slow, unsexy, glorious marathon of a study until its youngest participants are signing e-consent forms from their lunar retirement homes.

I think it’s bordering on scandalous that the National Portrait Gallery still needs to scrape together £100,000 to keep William Hoare’s portrait of Ayuba Suleiman Diallo—arguably the most electrifying riposte to 18th-century racial caricature—on these shores. In my view, every time I walk past the donation box I feel a twinge of embarrassment that a nation which once paraded Diallo through drawing rooms like a curiosity can’t now muster the price of a modest London flat to safeguard his image.  

Diallo—known in London salons as Job ben Solomon—was, as I see it, the original “exceptional” enslaved intellectual: a West African Muslim scholar kidnapped, shipped to America, yet still composing Arabic manuscripts in the hold. When Hoare painted him in 1733, he gave the sitter that steady, level gaze which, to me, seems to ask, “If you can meet my eye, why can’t you meet my freedom?” It’s arguably the first oil-on-canvas declaration that a black man’s mind and dignity were non-negotiable.  

So far, the gallery has raised a respectable chunk, but we’re still short. I can’t help wondering: if this were a lost Jane Austen doodle, wouldn’t the money have flooded in weeks ago? Corporations, foundations, ordinary visitors—myself included—need to dig deeper. Because, frankly, letting this portrait leave public hands would feel like ripping a hole in the story Britain tells about itself. And I, for one, don’t want to explain to my niece—who already asks why her school walls are so pale—that we lost the chance to keep Diallo’s face in the national mirror.

I think it’s impossible to stand on the edge of the Dajabón river at sunrise and not feel the weight of what I’m about to write. Their migration—if we can even reduce it to that bloodless word—is, in my view, a slow-motion catastrophe dressed up as opportunity. Exploitation? Arguably that’s the entry fee. Discrimination? It seems to me the daily weather. And exclusion—well, exclusion is the national sport on the Dominican side of the border, even if the government would rather call it sovereignty.

The Dominican Republic, richer than Haiti the way a broken tricycle is richer than a broken bicycle, still can’t feed its own under-employed masses. Yet Haitians keep coming, slipping through a border so porous I once watched a teenager wade across carrying a goat on his shoulders like it was nothing more than a commute. History, politics, economics—sure, those are the footnotes. But what I felt in the air was older than footnotes: a centuries-old sibling rivalry that turned vicious.

Here’s the twisted arithmetic: the DR needs cane cutters, brick carriers, toilet scrubbers—jobs that, frankly, most Dominicans I spoke to would rather endure poverty than accept. Enter the Haitians, who arguably keep the sugar industry alive. Yet the pay, I can tell you, is a pittance that vanishes the moment you buy a cold Presidente after twelve hours under a sun that doesn’t care about your visa status. And deportation? It hovers like a machete; I saw a foreman threaten to call immigration when a worker asked for water. How do you negotiate a raise when your bargaining chip is the right to stay in a country that pretends you aren’t there?

And then there are the children—some darker than others, all speaking Spanish with the same island lilt I grew up with—who discovered, courtesy of a 2013 Constitutional Court ruling that feels straight out of Kafka, that they are suddenly foreigners in the only country they’ve ever called home. Retroactive to 1929? In my view, that’s not law; that’s erasure with a legal seal. The United Nations can “express concern” until it’s blue in the face; I stood in a batey where a six-year-old showed me her birth certificate now officially worth less than the paper it’s printed on. Tell me, what do you say to a child who asks if she still exists?

To be fair—and I strain to be fair here—there are NGOs, church groups, even a handful of brave Dominican lawyers who keep chipping away. I trailed one young attorney who stuffed court appeals into a backpack that already held her lunch; she told me she keeps a spare phone charger because hearings drag on longer than hope. But the machinery they’re fighting is greased by overcrowded schools, hospitals at bursting point, and an economy that, from where I stood, feels one hurricane away from collapse.

Still, the buses roll out of Port-au-Prince every dawn. I shared a seat with a woman cradling a thermos of coffee and a plastic bag holding everything she owns. She admitted she’d been deported twice already. So why risk it again? She looked at me as if I’d asked why breathe. “Because tomorrow might be better,” she said—no manifesto, just stubborn optimism. If that isn’t the story of migration everywhere, I don’t know what is.

I think the silence that day felt almost unnatural—thick enough to choke on—as I watched the search teams crawl over the wreckage in their neon vests and plastic hats. Arguably, no hard hat in the world can protect you from the emotional shrapnel of knowing three of your own are still buried somewhere beneath that concrete sandwich.  

Work had slammed to a halt the moment the boiler house folded in on itself, and—let me be clear—it was the right call. But in my view, every hour investigators spent “assessing” translated into an eternity for the families pacing behind the cordon. I caught one woman staring at the pile as though sheer willpower could make it cough up her husband; how do you tell someone like that patience is a virtue?

Among the crew, emotions were splintered. Some whispered that maybe, just maybe, an air pocket had kept the men alive; others, eyes red-rimmed, looked like they’d already rehearsed the eulogies. I’ve covered disasters before, yet the cocktail of fear, guilt, and stubborn hope on this site still rattled me.  

The dogs—beautiful, single-minded animals—worked grid by grid, tails flicking like metronomes. Their handlers, stone-faced, rewarded them with quiet praise and a scratch behind the ears each time the animals paused, sniffed, then moved on. Meanwhile, investigators huddled over drone footage on a cracked laptop, pausing, rewinding, arguing about shadow versus void. It seems to me they were hunting for ghosts in pixels.

Overseeing it all stood the rescue chief, a man whose weathered cheeks should, by rights, earn him a quiet retirement. Instead, he carried the weight of three unknown graves. I caught his expression—jaw clenched, eyes glassy—and thought: that’s the face of someone who’s promised the impossible.

Yes, this day will scar the site’s history, but as dusk bled across the sky I saw something else: workers linking arms in a wordless vigil, helmets tucked under elbows, a makeshift family forged by tragedy. Call me sentimental, but I’d argue that raw solidarity counts as its own kind of rescue—if not of bodies, then of spirit.

I think it’s bordering on criminal that Scarthin Books – that labyrinthine paradise of second-hand paperbacks in Cromford – has had to plead for mercy from four steel columns just to stop its own stories from caving in. Arguably, when 100,000 books (a “few tons” is the politely vague estimate I keep hearing) start warping 200-year-old floorboards, you’ve reached the point where poetry meets physics, and physics always wins.  

It seems to me the rescue plan is as much about aesthetics as engineering: Stonewall and Hampstead, our local heritage-whisperers, swear the new supports will slip into the traffic flow “like quiet librarians” – but will they? I wandered the aisles last Saturday and kept imagining myself ducking around matte-grey pillars that weren’t there yet; I caught myself resenting the intrusion before it even happened.  

In my view, the firm’s track record is reassuring – they’ve resuscitated mills, chapels, even a temperance hall – yet I can’t shake the irony that a bookstore famous for its unruly, crooked charm now needs surgical-grade precision. Ventilation upgrades and beefed-up joists sound sensible enough, but do we really want our dusty, dog-eared sanctuary to feel… safe?  

The work will roll out in phases, we’re told, with crime shelved temporarily next to gardening, poetry shunted into the café. I picture loyal customers playing literary musical chairs, clutching their finds like refugees. Still, if the columns buy Scarthin another half-century of browsing bliss, who am I to grumble? After all, what’s the alternative – watch the ceiling sag until the last volume becomes the final straw?

I think it’s impossible to step into Carl James’s loft without feeling, well, slightly dizzy. There, wedged between towers of blaster-packing action figures and a life-sized cardboard Han Solo, the man himself—arguably Britain’s most obsessive Star Wars hoarder—grins like a kid who just found a tenner in an old coat. And, in a way, he did: a battered Boba Fett he snagged for 50p at a neighbour’s garage sale just netted him £15,000. Fifteen grand! For a piece of plastic that, let’s be honest, looks like it’s been chewed by a Wookiee. How does that not make the rest of us question every “worthless” box we’ve ever chucked?

Now Carl—soft-spoken, socks patterned with tiny X-wings—tells me he’s ready to liquidate the crown jewels: fifteen items, including what he swears is an authentic 32-inch Millennium Falcon filming model. I’m no appraiser, but when he lifts the tarp the room seems to glow; even the dust motes look star-struck. In my view, this isn’t just merch; it’s the celluloid DNA of my childhood. And yes, I felt a pang when he cradled that signed Vader helmet like a newborn, confessing, “It’s going to break my heart, mate, but hearts heal—mortgages don’t.”

Will the market bite? Arguably, yes. Star Wars collectors, a species who happily drop four figures on a scuffed Jawa, have already begun circling. Yet Carl insists sentiment still trumps cash. “Each piece is a memory,” he says, voice wobbling. I think he means it; I saw his eyes mist over a tiny Yoda, the rubber ears slightly askew. So why sell? Because, he shrugs, “stories want new owners.” Fair enough—though I wonder if the next bidder will love that Falcon as fiercely as the guy who kept it safe under a bed for three decades.

The auction, slated for next month, feels bigger than a roomful of storm-troopers. To me, it’s a referendum on nostalgia itself: proof that Lucas’s galaxy still binds us, merchandising and all. Researchers will watch, investors will salivate, and yes, I’ll be refreshing the bidding page at 2 a.m., half-hoping the prices tank so Carl keeps his treasures and the Force stays a private religion. But who am I kidding? If that Leia in her original cloak hits five digits, I’ll cheer—and then quietly mourn the moment memorabilia becomes just another asset class.

I think it’s nothing short of obscene that, in January, a teenager—whose name we still don’t know, and frankly I’m not sure we should protect—allegedly launched himself at Gwen Louden right there in the courthouse foyer, the one place you’re supposed to be blanketed by the rule of law. Arguably, the shock value is compounded by the fact that Ms. Louden, a woman I’ve watched host bake-sales that bankroll the local shelter, had simply shown up for what sources tell me was a routine small-claims squabble. Why her? I keep asking myself, and so, it seems, does she: friends say she keeps repeating, bewildered, “I still don’t understand why he picked me.”

Witnesses—most of whom, understandably, begged me not to print their names because our privacy statutes around minors and assault victims are, in my view, maddeningly strict—describe a blur of fists and no warning whatsoever. “He just attacked her without provocation,” one trembling bystander told me, and I could feel my own pulse racing as I scribbled the quote. Detective Francis Barnes, who struck me as genuinely rattled when we spoke, calls it “unprovoked,” but adds, rather hedgingly, that “all angles” remain open. Fair enough, yet what angle could possibly excuse decking a 60-something philanthropist beneath the marble gaze of Lady Justice?

Court security did pile in fast—faster, it seemed to me, than I’ve ever seen them move during my twenty years of sleepy morning arraignments—and the teen was instantly cuffed. Contempt-of-court charges followed; good, I say, though it feels like slapping a Band-Aid on a broken femur. Michelle Louden, Gwen’s daughter, fought back tears in the corridor, and I admit I had to pocket my notebook for a moment. “My mother is in her late sixties; it’s abhorrent,” she whispered, and I found myself nodding so vigorously my pen almost flew out the window.

Gwen is now recuperating in St. Luke’s; doctors tell me her vitals are stable, though I could see the purple blooming beneath her left eye when I peeked through the cracked door. Therapy, rest, privacy—her family’s plea is measured, but I sensed the fury vibrating beneath every syllable. Meanwhile, the accused slips into the Juvenile Justice maze, where, legal experts argue, he’ll likely be sentenced as a minor even if the assault and contempt charges stick. Is that justice? I’m honestly not sure.

And here’s the larger wound, the one that keeps me up at night: if a courthouse foyer—arguably the most surveilled square of real estate in town—can’t shield a Good Samaritan from a blindsiding, what hope do the rest of us have? Officials now promise a “security-protocol review,” but I’ve covered enough of these bureaucratic pledges to know the difference between a press-release Band-Aid and real, budget-biting change. Until we close this galling gap, public trust, in my view, will keep hemorrhaging right there on the courthouse steps.

I sat through every minute of the inquest, and I still can’t shake the image of a 37-year-old driver—Staley, from West Bridgford—deciding, in my view rather cavalierly, that a busy road was the perfect place to gun past another car. One moment of what investigators call, arguably generously, a “rash” manoeuvre, and Sally Shalloe—devoted mum, tireless volunteer, and the woman I used to nod hello to on my own weekend rides—was flung from her bike like a rag-doll.  

Do we honestly call that “an accident” when the speed limit is technically obeyed yet common sense is tossed out the window?

Eyewitnesses told me the thud still echoes in their ears; passers-by rushed in, paramedics arrived within minutes, but it seems to me the damage was sealed the instant Staley’s bumper clipped her wheel. Tom, her husband of 25 years, stood outside court clutching the arms of their two grown-up sons, Ben and Leo, and said—voice cracking—that Sally was “the heart of our family.” I think every reporter within earshot swallowed hard; I know I did.

Yes, Staley was under the limit, but investigators argue, and I happen to agree, that overtaking there was “potentially dangerous.” Charges of causing death by dangerous driving followed, and next week Nottingham Crown Court will decide whether the law agrees with what, in my view, the rest of us already feel: that a split-second of impatient acceleration can amount to manslaughter on wheels.

Walk through Attenborough now and you’ll see bouquets still wired to the railings, a ghost bike painted white, and, arguably, a village trying to stitch itself back together. Hundreds packed the memorial; I spotted toddlers on stabilisers and pensioners with walking sticks, all insisting Sally would want us to keep pedalling. Plans for a cycle path in her name sound lovely—yet I wonder, will a strip of asphalt really soothe a family’s grief or simply let council minutes boast a “legacy”?

Sally’s decades with the wildlife trust, her dawn litter-picks, her laugh at the village-coffee mornings—those memories linger longer than any tarmac. Still, if her death forces council engineers and MPs to rethink lane widths and overtaking bans, then, arguably, her life won’t have ended in vain. I think we owe her that much, don’t we?

I think we’ve all seen this movie before—literally. The red carpet, the blinding flashbulbs, the same recycled “who are you wearing?” refrain. Yet here I was, squashed between a boom-mic operator and a woman clutching a life-size cardboard cut-out of Chris Pine, wondering: does glamour ever get bored with itself?  

Arguably, the hype machine rolled in on schedule: private jets disgorged A-listers who’d flown, what, three hours to travel 15 miles? In my view, their smiles looked air-brushed on; I caught one Oscar-winning actress practicing hers in the tinted window of her SUV. The fans—bless them—had camped since dawn, clutching dog-eared posters and throat-lozenge wrappers, their enthusiasm so raw it made my cynical heart twitch.  

Inside, the theater smelled of fresh popcorn and nervous cologne. I snagged an aisle seat and eavesdropped on two producers calculating opening-weekend “conservative” estimates that still sounded like phone numbers. Word was we’d get a quick speech from the leads—though, between you and me, I’ve heard more spontaneity from my GPS.  

When the cast finally sauntered down the side aisle, the room hushed like a third-grade classroom promised extra recess. They signed a few programs, posed for selfies that will be filtered into oblivion within minutes, and answered press questions so smoothly I suspect Siri ghost-writes for them. Their excitement felt genuine, or genuinely well-rehearsed—who can tell anymore?  

Cocktails kept materializing in my hand; I swear the ushers were undercover mixologists. Gowns shimmered, cufflinks winked, and conversations swirled around backend percentages and after-party RSVPs. It seems to me the real screenplay being workshopped wasn’t on-screen but in the lobby whispers.  

By dusk, the city beyond the velvet ropes had blurred into mere backdrop. The red carpet lay abandoned, littered with souvenir wristbands and the odd stiletto that didn’t survive the photo pit. Box-office prophets were already polishing their headlines, but for two suspended hours none of that mattered. The lights dimmed; my notebook rustled. I caught myself holding my breath—maybe, just maybe, the film itself could justify the circus.  

And then the first frame flickered, the room exhaled, and even I—professional skeptic—felt the hush. The show was finally, mercifully, underway.

I think the second half began with one of those momentum-killing Gloucester penalties that, frankly, make me wonder why anyone still calls rugby a “running game.” Sure, it nudged the hosts ahead, but—call me biased—it felt like a spreadsheet creeping across the pitch rather than sport.  

Then, hallelujah, Jack Nowell reminded us what wings are for, diving into the corner like a man who’d read my private diary of frustrations. Exeter, in my view, finally played with the audacity I’d been craving, hammering away in wave after wave. Yet Gloucester’s defence, stubborn as a rainy British summer, held firm. Is there anything more teeth-grinding than watching courage smothered by organisation?

With twenty-odd minutes left, Billy Twelvetrees—whose name I’ve always found suspiciously musical for a rugby player—slotted another three. Arguably, that should have been curtains. But the Chiefs kept flinging themselves about, and, for a moment, I swear the Shed held its breath when Nic White scooted under the posts. 25-15: hope, that mischievous imp, peeked through the clouds.

When Sam Simmonds bulldozed over late on, I actually leapt from my plastic seat—notebook flying, dignity forgotten. Five points adrift with time ticking? Why not dream? Alas, Willie Heinz ripped the script from my hands and dotted down almost immediately. Game, set, and in my humble opinion, a rather cruel anti-climax.

So, no miracle finish. Exeter’s effort was, I think, the dictionary definition of valiant; Gloucester’s 30-20 win the dictionary definition of efficient. Afterwards, Johan Ackermann praised everyone in sight—standard coach-speak, though I sensed genuine relief beneath the clichés.

The victory arguably nudges Gloucester’s playoff pulse from flicker to flame, and I, for one, will be eyeing their trip to Saracens with popcorn ready. Exeter? They’ve been handed a reality check stamped in neon. If they don’t tighten every last nut against Harlequins, the top four could slip away faster than a scrum-half’s tap-penalty.

I think it’s impossible to stare at this firm’s balance sheet without feeling a jolt of dread: a pension black hole so vast it’s swallowing every spare pound that ought to be fuelling growth. In my view, management is effectively bailing out a bathtub with a thimble; no matter how much they’ve poured in—arguably heroic sums, I’d say—low interest rates and wobbly markets keep punching fresh holes in the hull. So, what else can they do? Off-load the whole liability to the PPF or, if the gatekeepers smile on the deal, to some sharp-suited insurer that traffics in pension risk? On paper, yes, that would scrub the scarlet ink off the books and—let’s be candid—free executives to chase sexier, higher-margin ventures.  

Yet, and this strikes me as crucial, we’re not talking about swapping a rusty fleet van here; we’re talking about people’s retirements, the deferred wages of lifetimes spent on factory floors or in open-plan cubicles. Regulators must therefore ask, I think, whether the assets backing those promises are more hologram than hard cash. And, frankly, do we trust the PPF—an outfit designed for corporate corpses—to play hospice to a still-breathing company without squeezing the life out of future benefits?  

Walking the corridors last week, I sensed a low-grade anxiety that no corporate newsletter can massage away. Employees cornered me—off the record, naturally—to wonder if “protected” is just legalese for “you’ll get something, but don’t ask how much.” The union reps, sleeves rolled up, argue—arguably correctly—that transparency shouldn’t be a bargaining chip; it should be the price of admission to any negotiation.  

So here we stand, waiting for a handful of civil-servant actuaries to bless or block the grand escape plan. I, for one, can’t shake the feeling that whatever decision lands in the next few weeks will ripple far beyond this single company: it will sketch a roadmap for every other boardroom staring at a pension abyss. And if the answer is no? Well, then management may have to confront the uncomfortable question they’ve dodged for a decade: how did we let the promise of a dignified retirement mutate into a balance-sheet ogre in the first place?

I think it’s impossible to read about Otto Warmbier’s final journey without feeling a knot in your stomach. Here was a 21-year-old University of Virginia student—arguably guilty of nothing more than youthful curiosity—who joined a tour group in January 2016 and, in my view, walked straight into a Stalinist nightmare. North Korean state media, never a paragon of transparency, labeled his alleged crime “hostile acts” and slapped him with a 15-year hard-labor sentence. Fifteen years? For, what, trying to steal a propaganda poster? It seems to me the regime needed a fresh American bargaining chip, and Warmbier was unlucky enough to fit the costume.

Fast-forward 17 months: last week the same government that imprisoned him suddenly shipped him home in a persistent vegetative state. His parents’ announcement on Tuesday—that their son had died only six days after arrival—felt like a punch the entire country took to the gut. I found myself staring at the headline, wondering the obvious: how does a healthy college kid return in a coma, and why did Pyongyang wait until the final hour to release him? A US coroner is now scrambling for answers, but I’d wager we’ll be left with more hedged medical jargon than hard facts.

President Trump, never shy of superlatives, called the North’s treatment “brutal” and vowed to “prevent such tragedies.” In my view, that statement lands somewhere between genuine outrage and calculated messaging—after all, his administration is already hunting for leverage against Kim’s missile fetish. Still, who among us wouldn’t want to believe Washington can shield the next Otto?

Pyongyang’s explanation—that botulism plus a sleeping pill induced the coma—strikes me, and apparently every American doctor who examined him, as insultingly facile. The evidence I’ve seen reported points toward a traumatic brain injury, the kind that doesn’t just happen in custody unless something went horrifically wrong. Are we honestly expected to accept that a bacterial toxin neatly timed itself to erase a prisoner’s consciousness right after sentencing?

Unsurprisingly, Warmbier’s death has poured rocket fuel on already smoldering US–North Korea tensions. Trump, I suspect, will use the tragedy to press Congress for harsher sanctions, and I think many lawmakers—Republican and Democrat alike—will oblige. Yet sanctions, arguably, have done little so far to deter Kim’s nuclear march. So tell me: what response, short of war, actually rattles a regime that seems to value human life so cheaply?

Richard Howitt – who, I think, has been parked in the East of England’s European Parliament seat since 1994 – is, arguably, swapping one Brussels-style acronym for another by grabbing the CEO title at the International Integrated Reporting Council. The IIRC, a sprawling coalition of regulators, investors, bean-counters and NGOs, wants, in its own jargon, to “link corporations with society.” Fine, but does anyone outside the conference circuit actually feel linked?

In my view, Howitt’s mission is to make integrated reporting the new normal: a single document that supposedly marries profit, planet and governance so we mortals can see the company whole. I’ve sat through enough sustainability briefings to know the concept is noble – yet the spreadsheets still smell of creative air-freshener. Still, Howitt has banged the CSR drum for decades, so the fit feels, well, predestined.

“I’m honoured,” he told reporters – and, honestly, who wouldn’t be? – promising to herd the world’s boardrooms toward “global adoption of integrated frameworks.” Translation: he wants firms to confess their carbon sins and social slip-ups in the same breath as their cash-flow brags. Noble, yes, but will it survive the first quarterly-earnings panic? I have my doubts.

Howitt insists he’ll keep clocking in at the Parliament until the baton officially passes; I’ve seen MEPs juggle worse. Meanwhile, IIRC chair Mervyn King (no, not the Bank-of-England one) gushed that Howitt’s “passion” is a perfect match. From where I sit, that sounds like code for “he knows every corridor in Brussels and can translate bureaucratese into English.”

He’s been on the IIRC council since its 2010 birth and moonlights as the Parliament’s CSR rapporteur – credentials that, arguably, make him the safest pair of hands in a very small field. To me, the switch signals that integrated reporting is sliding from NGO wish-list to boardroom checklist; whether that curbs corporate mischief or merely sprinkles green glitter on it remains, frustratingly, an open question.

David Waddington—yes, I’m afraid that’s another name from the Tory pantheon—was, in my view, the very embodiment of pin-striped gravitas wrapped around a tongue sharp enough to fillet you at twenty paces. Born, as the record books insist, on 2 August 1929 in Burnley, he parlayed a legal training into what I think we’re meant to call “statesmanship” inside the Westminster bubble.  

He first popped up as MP for Nelson and Colne in 1968—arguably a quieter corner of the world than he deserved—before shifting to the altogether plusher pastures of Ribble Valley from 1983 to 1990. Thatcher, never one to miss a useful Yorkshire terrier of discipline, duly handed him the Chief Whip’s cosh and, later, the whole Home Office.  

Now, spring 1990: I was on the Strand that day, nose stinging from tear-gas, notebook soaked, and I remember thinking—how on earth does anyone “manage” a 25-day prison revolt and simultaneous street insurrection over the poll tax? Strangeways erupted first: prisoners, sick of slopping-out and medieval overcrowding, took the roof and held it for nearly a month. Two dead, scores injured, and Waddington—arguably looking paler than his usual marble—ordered the Tactical Firearms Group in. Control was regained, yes, and a certain Woolf Report followed, but at what human cost?  

Meanwhile, Trafalgar Square looked like a medieval melee. I saw police horses charge lines of kids clutching Socialist Worker placards; I saw bricks arc over the National Gallery steps. Critics, myself included at the time, denounced the minister’s stance as heavy-handed; supporters countered that only a “firm hand” could save the realm. Which narrative sticks? Depends, I suppose, on whether you were nursing a head-wound or cheering from the Carlton Club.  

Thatcher’s sudden defenestration later that year swept Waddington upstairs—literally—to the Lords, where John Major parked him as Leader of the House. In 2 he became Baron Waddington of Read, retired to the shires, and, I think, never quite forgave the world for questioning his judgment.  

Love him or loathe him—and I’ve veered between the two over three decades—his fingerprints are still visible on today’s prison-reform debates and, whisper it, on the poll tax’s quick demise. A staunch traditionalist? Undeniably. A man who shaped Britain’s early-’90s mood? Arguably, yes—though whether that shape resembles a shield or a bludgeon is, to me, still an open wound.

I think it’s nothing short of a national disgrace that, in a country which prides itself on fair play, roughly one million older people are left to fend for themselves. Arguably, the raft of policies trumpeted by ministers is little more than glossy wallpaper pasted over a crumbling wall: one-third of elderly citizens who need help are, in my view, invisible to the very system meant to protect them. I’ve watched neighbours rationing tablets and skipping meals, and I keep asking—how is this acceptable in 2024?

The report says 700,000 of the 1.5 million over-65s with unmet needs receive absolutely no help at all. It seems to me that “unmet” is bureaucratic shorthand for “abandoned”. When an elderly person falls at home because there’s no one to answer the call bell, the bruises aren’t just physical; they’re moral marks on us all. In my experience, the loneliness that follows is corrosive: one gentleman told me he sets an alarm every three hours just to hear a human voice—his own—because no one else will speak to him all day.

Yes, the population is ageing rapidly, but that’s hardly a surprise announcement. Governments have seen this grey wave on the horizon for decades and, in my view, chose to whistle past the graveyard. Now the tsunami is here, and it’s swamping A&E departments because early, cheaper care never materialised. I’ve stood in hospital corridors where frail patients wait 12 hours for a bed that should have been freed by social care at home; it feels like watching dominoes fall in slow motion.

Age UK, rightly in my view, demands that older people and their families co-design whatever comes next. I’d go further: let’s put a retired teacher, a part-time carer and an 80-year-old diabetic on the panel—because right now the “consultations” I’ve attended smell like tokenism. Plugging today’s gaps means emergency grants for cash-strapped families, a single telephone line that actually picks up, and wages that keep care workers from fleeing the sector.  

And funding? Arguably, if we can find billions for roads and rail, we can find cash for the people who once built this country. In my view, refusing to pay now is a false economy that will bankrupt both the NHS and our collective conscience. So I’ll keep asking: if we’re content to let older citizens suffer quietly behind closed doors, what does that say about the rest of us?

I think it’s impossible to hear about Gomez and not feel a stab of guilt for every caged animal we’ve ever walked past. Since the tiny marmoset’s discovery on a vet’s doorstep—abandoned, trembling, arguably one heartbeat away from becoming another anonymous casualty—my inbox, and I suspect yours, has been flooded with petitions, donation links, and outraged emojis. How did we let this happen… again?

As I understand it, Gomez is the lone survivor of a whole family shipped to a backyard “zoo” that, in my view, never deserved its license. When the place folded last year, the owners simply shrugged—no contingency plan, no shame. A local rescue group scooped up most of the cast-offs, yet somehow the marmosets slipped through the cracks. One by one, they vanished; I can’t help picturing them fading like ghosts into the pine scrub, until only Gomez remained.

Whoever left him at the clinic door apparently expected applause for not dumping him in a ditch. The vet team tells me he was so dehydrated his skin “tented,” and, heartbreakingly, he startles at his own shadow. Police have opened an investigation; good, but in my experience these cases stall unless public rage stays white-hot. Hence the reward kitty—donations from strangers like me who’d rather fund justice than buy another latte.

Right now Gomez clings to a plush toy the size of his lost sisters; it seems to me that floppy monkey is the only thing keeping his little psyche stitched together. Rehab staff whisper progress reports—he ate a full grape today, let a keeper scratch his neck—but I catch the caveat: “slow process.” Translation: years, maybe, before he trusts anything with a pulse.

Meanwhile, lawmakers are scrambling to table “Gomez’s Law,” which, if you ask me, is political theater until the ink dries. Yes, we need tighter oversight of private menageries, and yes, every shuttered zoo should be legally required to rehome its inmates before padlocking the gate. But haven’t we promised that before?

The silver lining, if one can call it that, is the sudden donor frenzy for Atlantic-forest conservation. My social feed is all big eyes and fluffy ears; marmoset memes apparently pry open wallets faster than graphs of deforestation. I’ll take it—though I wonder whether we need a fresh tragedy every few months to keep the spotlight from swinging away.

So here we are, a nation collectively cooing over a single rescued primate while thousands of his wild cousins lose another acre of habitat to soy fields. I think we’re better than that, but arguably the mirror Gomez holds up is cracked—and it reflects us.

I think it’s nothing short of a miracle that no one was hurt, but—honestly—how many more heritage-listed pubs have to burn before we treat empty buildings as something more than kindling? Shortly after 9 p.m. last night I was walking my dog past the corner of St. Mary’s Street when I saw the first orange lick of flame shooting from the roof of the old White Hart. In my view, it was already too late; within an hour the place was a furnace.

Roger Jenkins, the South Wales fire spokesperson, later told me—rather calmly, I thought—that 30 firefighters, six engines, an aerial ladder and a water carrier had been scrambled from as far afield as Pontypridd. “Severe and well-established,” he called it, which seems to me a polite way of saying the building was toast. Still, credit where it’s due: they stopped the fire jumping to the terraces on either side, arguably saving the whole block.

Neighbours in dressing-gowns and slippers shivered in the community hall while Red Cross volunteers dispensed tea that, I confess, tasted like wet cardboard. We were allowed back at dawn; the smell of charred timber clung to my coat all day. Jenkins says the roof and first floor are gone, and I think that’s an optimistic way of describing a pile of smoking rafters. Arson? Not ruled out, they say—yet can anyone remember the last time an empty 300-year-old pub spontaneously combusted?

The White Hart has stood since the 1700s, shuttered lately but supposedly on the cusp of renovation. I’d looked forward to boasting that my round was poured in the same snugs where navvies once brawled. Now the police tape flutters like bunting at a funeral, and the investigators pick through ashes. Still, the neighbourhood WhatsApp group is already buzzing with pledges—arguably quixotic, but heart-warming all the same—to raise what it takes to rebuild. In my view, we’d better hurry; heritage, like smoke, has a habit of drifting away.

Nelson Packaging’s board, I think, would like us to read yesterday’s redundancy announcement as a sad-but-necessary surgical cut. Arguably, it felt more like a hacksaw taken to a factory that, in my view, had already been limping through the global slump. I drove past the Lancashire site at dawn and saw the car park half-empty; even the security guard, a man I’ve chatted to for years, looked like he was rehearsing his own P45 speech.  

The company line—delivered in that bloodless corporate passive voice—is that “redundancies were a necessary course of action.” Necessary for whom, exactly? The 200-odd production and admin staff I’ve interviewed over coffee in the canteen certainly weren’t consulted. One technician told me, voice cracking, that he’d just remortgaged to keep the family afloat. Multiply that by every workstation now dark and you begin to grasp, I think, why union reps are calling this a body-blow to a county already on life-support.  

Union banners outside the gate accuse management of “pandemic opportunism.” Harsh? Perhaps. But it seems to me that if you axe 18 % of your payroll while simultaneously booking £3.2 m in Covid bounce-back loans, you should expect some righteous anger. The local MP—who, full disclosure, is a friend of mine from constituency surgeries—put it bluntly: “We need Whitehall rescue money yesterday.” Will Westminster listen? Past form suggests the Treasury’s wallet snaps shut the moment you cross the M62.
